Scale bar, approximately 65 µm. f, pCT images after 1-N preload (left) and 50-µm compressive displacement (Comp.; right). Scale bars, 300 µm. g, 3D rendering of a sub-volume used for DVC tracking between images (left), and sub-volume after translation, rotation and the first order strain to match the deformed image (right). h, Illustration of the point cloud before (left) and after (right) compression, demonstrating different modes of tissue and fibre deformation.

Next, the 3D orientation and estimated scattering amplitude of fibres are used to perform an iterative simulation of the SAXS tomography and isolate angularly independent scattering instances (Methods; Fig. 2c, top panel). By fitting SAXS profiles with 3D diffraction models1, the physical parameters fibril D-period, D-period variation and fibril diameter (Fig. 1d) can be obtained for each fibre (Methods; Fig. 2c, middle and bottom panels). Reconstruction follows a cascading pattern, in which the solution of individual fibres enables further deconvolution of neighbouring fibres, allowing an iterative sweep through the sample until every possible fibre has been fitted. Fibril properties can then be mapped onto the pCT image, enabling assessment of spatial variation and gradients in nanoscale properties (Methods; Fig. 2d).

The measurement of strain from per-fibre nanoscale properties requires accurate tracking of fibre deformation during in situ experimentation; achieved here with DVC analysis4,21,22,24. DVC analysis was performed on pCT datasets to measure the deformation of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus following axial compression using a local, sub-volume based approach, with measurement points placed along the traced fibres (Methods; Fig. 2e,f). Application of DVC-measured displacements to traced fibres in their undeformed state allows calculation of their location and orientation following loading, while preserving fibre index. This information is used to reconstruct SAXS data of loaded fibres and compare resultant fibrillar parameters across loading to generate nanoscale strain values. Fibre-level and tissue-level strains can also be obtained from the DVC-measured displacements (Methods; Fig. 2f).

To establish and validate the fundamental principles of the TomoSAXS reconstruction method, initial validation experiments were performed on a simple construct of dried chicken foot tendons using laboratory X-ray sources. Three tendons were dried under different levels of tensile load to create uniformly oriented bundles of collagen fibres with different D-periods (Methods; Extended Data Fig. 2). The results showed an increased D-period and D-period variation in the tendon dried under the highest tensile strain (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h), fibril strains of 0.6–2.8% and an effective fibril modulus of approximately 0.2 GPa, in the same range as previous single-fibril measurements34, demonstrating the ability of TomoSAXS to resolve variations in nanoscale collagen properties in a known system.

The accuracy of TomoSAXS for estimating nanoscale parameters in the rat IVD has been tested using digital phantoms (Extended Data Fig. 3). We created a series of digital IVD phantoms using indexed fibre geometries from three real samples and applying synthetic nanoscale fibrillar properties (Extended Data Fig. 3ai–ii). By applying noise in measured background scattering intensity from real SAXS frames (Extended Data Fig. 3aiii,av) to simulated signals under analysis (Extended Data Fig. 3aiv–vi), we estimated how accurately the TomoSAXS reconstruction reproduces the known parameters. We found significant correlation between reconstructed and ground-truth data (P < 0.001, r2 = 0.641–0.894). Accuracy, measured as the mean absolute error (Methods), was 1.032 nm for the mean D-period (6.8% of the 6σ width), 0.280 nm for D-period variation (4.2% of the 6σ width) and 8.532 nm for fibril diameter (6.9 % of the 6σ width). Precision, measured as the standard deviation of absolute error (Methods), was 1.37 nm for the mean D-period (9.05% of the 6σ width), 0.34 nm for D-period variation (5.1% of the 6σ width) and 15.32 nm for fibril diameter (6.9% of the 6σ width). Comparison of mapped known versus estimated properties also suggest that spatial patterns in known properties are reconstructed (Extended Data Fig. 3b–d). When provided noise-free data on identical geometries, TomoSAXS reconstruction accuracy improved, with r2 = 0.874–0.915, which demonstrates the theoretical limitations of the technique (Supplementary Fig. 8).

TomoSAXS correlates 3D microscale imaging with nanoscale measurements from SAXS, enabling 3D mapping and direct statistical comparison of per-fibre microscale and nanoscale properties in macroscopic samples. Here application of TomoSAXS resulted in 3D maps of structural and mechanical properties specific to individual collagen fibres across the spatiostructural hierarchy of the annulus fibrosus (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The orientational texture of our samples and applied experimental parameters (Methods) permitted nanoscale reconstruction for more than 55% of all fibres within the scanned volume (Supplementary Fig. 6). This provided sufficient resolution to highlight complex textural patterns in both structural and mechanical nanoscale properties (Fig. 3c,e and Extended Data Fig. 4l–q).

a, Tissue-level patterns in compression (third principal strain ε3; top) and tension (first principal strain ε1; bottom). b, Microscale fibre strain patterns in the anterior (top) and posterior (bottom) annulus fibrosis. c, Nanoscale patterns in the initial D-period showing anticorrelation with fibre strain patterns in panel b. Scale bars represent 300 µm. d, 3D reconstruction of fibre strain patterns through the entire annulus fibrosis. e, Maps of nanoscale properties found within the region in panel d marked with yellow dashed lines. f, Two-sided linear regression analysis of fibre curvature versus fibre strain magnitude (left; n = 9,326; r2 = 0.480; P = 0.0001); the fibrillar D-period strain versus the fibre strain (middle; n = 1,826; r2 = 0.138; P = 0.0010); and the fibrillar D-period strain versus the initial D-period (right; n = 1,826; r2 = 0.312; P = 0.0001). The pink dashed line denotes the 95% confidence interval (CI), and the purple dashed line indicates the prediction interval (PI). The green box plots represent standard deviations across both axes for evenly spaced subsamples across the x axis, centred around the mean of each respective subsample across both axes (f). No adjustments were made for multiple comparisons. All images are from a single representative IVD (IVD1).

An estimated 100-nm accuracy in DVC fibre-displacement tracking (Methods) allowed confident estimations of displacement under load for individual fibres, enabling precise per-fibre nanoscale D-period and fibril diameter strain measurements (Fig. 3e, bottom panel, and Extended Data Fig. 4m,o,q). The nanoscale measurements of structure and mechanical response can then be directly compared with those at the fibre and tissue levels (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 4).

At the highest level (Fig. 3a), local tissue strains measured from the DVC were overall higher than the bulk strain applied to the IVD, measured as the percentage change in disc height (Methods; Supplementary Note 8). A reduction in IVD height of 2.2% resulted in tissue-level principal compressive strains of 4.2 ± 3.3% in the annulus fibrosus28 (Fig. 3a, top panel); local tissue strains higher than the overall applied strain have been observed in other hard-soft tissue junctions2.

Maps of tissue-level first principal (tensile) strain reveal both lamellar and trans-lamellar patterns (Fig. 3a, bottom panel). Projecting tissue-level strain along the circumferential direction (Extended Data Fig. 5a) shows alternating trans-lamellar bands of tension and compression (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We hypothesize that these strain patterns may be related to the trans-lamellar cross-bridging network of the annulus fibrosus (Extended Data Fig. 5b), as previously suggested21, which is thought to aid in returning annulus fibrosus tissue to its original shape after deformation20. Because strains were recorded after stress relaxation, these trans-lamellar patterns may be a result of elastic recoil from the inter-lamellar matrix. Such patterns suggest that trans-lamellar cross-bridges may be an initiation site for annular tears, providing support for previous hypotheses35. Spatial mapping of strain in the radial direction shows clear radial compression of the annulus fibrosus due to bulging of the nucleus pulposus (Extended Data Fig. 5d), with some lamellae exhibiting radial tension, possibly due to swelling induced by fluid flow out of the nucleus pulposus into the annulus fibrosus36.

Tissue-level principal strain direction, measured as the angle between the strain eigenvector and the local fibre tangent (Extended Data Fig. 5g), averaged 55 ± 22° for compression and 58 ± 21° for tension (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Fibres resist tensile strains aligned with their orientation but provide little resistance to strain in other directions. The lack of alignment between tissue-level principal strains and fibre orientation therefore indicates substantial strain accommodation by the extrafibrillar matrix and inter-fibre motion. Spatial mapping of principal strain directions shows clear lamellar texturing, with alternating lamellae demonstrating tissue-level principal strains acting parallel or orthogonal to the fibre direction (Extended Data Fig. 5f,h).

Fibre-level strain magnitude showed a significant positive correlation with fibre curvature (r2 = 0.480, P < 0.001; Fig. 3f, left panel, and Extended Data Fig. 5i,j). Fibres with the greatest curvature were typically located at the transition zone between the nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus in the posterior and lateral regions of the IVD (Extended Data Fig. 5j), with these fibres showing a tendency to increase in curvature under compressive loading of the IVD (Extended Data Fig. 5k). The link between fibre curvature and fibre strain may partially explain why the posterior and posterior–lateral regions of the IVD are most prone to herniation37.

Fibre strain measured from the DVC showed a significant positive correlation with fibrillar D-period strain measured from SAXS (r2 = 0.138, P < 0.001; Fig. 3f, middle panel). A mean fibre strain magnitude equal to 3.70% (±3.19%) and mean fibrillar strain magnitude equal to 3.60% (±3.36%) suggests that most of the strain at the fibre level is passed down to the fibril, with limited inter-fibril sliding at this level of loading. However, the slope of the regression line deviates from one due to a distinct subpopulation of fibres with near-zero D-period strain, which experience a considerably higher fibre strain magnitude (Fig. 3f, middle panel). This may be evidence of previously reported lags in fibril strain response to low-strain conditions due to molecular tilting in twisted collagen fibres38.

Fibrillar D-period strain showed a significant negative correlation with the initial fibrillar D-period (r2 = 0.312, P < 0.001; Fig. 3f, right panel). This can be interpreted as IVD tissues with fibres under initial tensile pre-strain undergoing compression upon loading, and those with an initial compressive pre-strain undergoing tension. Although it seems counterintuitive, at the nanoscale, where strain is measured over lengths of approximately 67 nm in fibrils with diameters of 20–120 nm, collagen fibrils can support compressive loading, with the surrounding extrafibrillar matrix providing lateral support that suppresses buckling.

The initial fibrillar D-period covered a broad range of values: from 60 nm to 74 nm. Assuming a zero-strain state of approximately 67 nm, this represents residual fibrillar strains ranging from −10% to +10% in the IVD. Given a Young’s modulus of approximately 1–2 GPa for hydrated type I collagen fibrils34, our data translate to a measured pre-stress of 100–200 MPa. The measured failure stress of single collagen fibrils from rat tendons range from 70 to 200 MPa39, indicating that residual stress in the IVD may result in fibrillar strains close to failure. This may help to explain why the annulus fibrosus is susceptible to microdamage at mechanical loads well below those required to induce failure in the disc40. Similar high pre-stresses have been reported before for tendon collagen and mineralized collagen fibrils41,42, and may be required to adapt material stiffness to meet the challenging mechanical requirements of the IVD. The regression line for the initial D-period versus the D-period strain shows that D-period strain values typically return the fibril D-period towards its zero-strain state of 67 nm.

The mean fibrillar D-period demonstrated a significant positive correlation with intra-fibrillar variation in the D-period (r2 = 0.089, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). Fibrils with larger mean D-periods, which can be considered as having a tensile pre-strain, have greater variability in the D-periods of their constituent microfibrils. We also found a significant negative relationship between initial per-fibre D-period variation and change in variation upon load (r2 = 0.340, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 6), suggesting that fibres undergoing compression become less variable in the D-period and the inverse for those undergoing tension.

Global and spatial patterns in structural and mechanical properties at the fibril to tissue level can be analysed by the spatial registration of TomoSAXS datasets. The mean fibril diameter exhibits twofold or larger variability across the tissue (64.4 ± 32.5 nm), with a clear lamellar texture (Fig. 3e, top panel). Closer inspection of fibril diameter distribution (Extended Data Fig. 7h) reveals multiple peaks on a base harmonic of approximately 20 nm. This aligns with previous electron microscopy studies43 revealing type II collagen fibrils form different super-coiled structures from a building block of repeated approximately 20-nm microfibrils. Combined with the texture seen in Fig. 3e (top panel), these results suggest that super-coiling levels may be different in different regions of the annulus fibrosus and between lamellae.

Algorithmic straightening of maps44 for fibrillar-level properties permits comparison of their spatial patterns across individual transects through the annulus fibrosus via line profiles, providing quantitative support for correlations qualitatively visualized between fibril characteristics and their lamellar texture (Extended Data Fig. 8). Of note, comparisons of the D-period pre-strain and fibre orientation (α) across shared transects through the posterior annulus fibrosus suggest that pre-strain is broadly conserved within individual lamellae, and neighbouring lamellae show contrasting pre-strains suggestive of complementary fibrillar pre-stress (Extended Data Fig. 8).

We demonstrated the potential of the TomoSAXS technique on human samples, by performing correlative hierarchical phase-contrast tomography (HiP-CT)45 and tomographic SAXS at high energies on a whole formalin-fixed IVD (approximately 5 cm width) at The European Synchrotron. A single-slice reconstruction of the data shows clear texturing of nanoscale properties (Fig. 4e). The measured D-period ranged from 62.38 to 73.80 nm with a mean value of 67.15 nm (standard deviation = 0.98 nm), D-period variation ranged from 0.175 to 3.07 nm with a mean value of 1.56 nm (standard deviation = 0.61 nm) and fibril diameter ranged from 15.67 to 117.78 nm with a mean value of 41.29 nm (standard deviation = 17.08 nm). This represents an order of magnitude increase in sample dimensions probed using 3D SAXS techniques and opens doors for the investigation of matrix drivers of health and disease in intact human organs.

a, Complete human spine. b, Fibre tracing generated from HiP-CT of an intact human IVD (thoracic level 11–12, 64-year-old male donor). c, High-energy SAXS pattern. d, Greyscale HiP-CT image showing a clear fibre texture (top) and a zoomed-in image of a region of fibre-tracing data (bottom). e, Single-slice TomoSAXS reconstruction showing the D-period (left), D-period variation (middle) and fibril diameter (right) across the IVD. f, Schematic outlining the mechanisms of load transfer isolated here from the macrolevel or whole-tissue level, to the nanoscale.

The TomoSAXS methodology provides an unparalleled view of macroscale-to-nanoscale mechanics in the IVD (Fig. 4c). By embedding SAXS data within the structural and mechanical context from pCT and DVC, it enables analysis of nanoscale–tissue interactions within the hierarchical assembly of the IVD. Tissue-level strains show complex patterns, probably linked to non-collagenous annulus fibrosus components such as elastin, thought to enable recoiling of the annulus fibrosus after deformation20. Fibre-level strains showed a strong correlation with fibre curvature, indicating that highly curved regions may be more prone to injury.

Fibrillar mechanics critically inform strain transmission across scales. Fibrillar pre-strains (initial D-period) and load-induced strain showed strong spatial relationships with fibre-level strains. Their absolute magnitudes suggest that most fibre strain is transferred directly to fibrils, with little inter-fibrillar shear, unlike tendons under tension46. Avoiding the averaging effect of commonly used 2D diffraction techniques for studying nanoscale strains and the convolution of scattering from fibres at differing orientations (Extended Data Fig. 9) may also contribute to the wider spread of fibril strains seen (up to approximately 10–15%), which are consistent with tensile tests of individual fibrils39.

A negative correlation between the initial D-period and D-period strain suggests pre-strained fibrils converge towards a neutral state under load. High fibrillar residual stresses position the IVD in a mechanically advantageous but vulnerable state. This correlates with clinically seen high levels of degeneration in the IVD13,14,15,16. Pre-strain stiffens an otherwise compliant tissue, enabling physiological load bearing while reducing the remaining margin before damaging strains are reached. This illustrates a fundamental trade-off in fibre-reinforced biological tissues, in which mechanical performance is achieved at the expense of increased susceptibility to microdamage and degeneration.

The relationship between mean and variance in per-fibre D-period supports a helical coil model of fibrillar mechanics, loosening or tightening under load (Fig. 4f), akin to previous twisted or coiled fibre models38,47. This suggests an increase in the variability of stress along fibres as they deviate from a purely compressive (lowest possible D-period) state (Fig. 4f). In this scenario, loading causes increased local swelling pressure to a fibril in a low D-period state, leading to localized regions of high tension (and higher D-period), a phenomenon that is amplified as overall osmotic pressure and residual strain increases. Loss of residual strain in the IVD leads to aberrant cellular mechanosensing and degeneration48; however, methods to measure fibrillar-level pre-strain in intact organs have been lacking until now.

The multiscale mechanisms of load response reported here may be incorporated into finite-element modelling of IVD biomechanics49 and explain complex non-linear load responses. Collagen fibrils store stress and strain energy through osmotic pressure shifts, generating hundreds of MPa during dehydration42. These correlations have potential clinical relevance in musculoskeletal degeneration, with reduction in swelling pressure due to synthetic ageing shown to result in a reduction of fibrillar pre-strain in articular cartilage50. The mean values and load-induced changes of nanoscale properties reported here conform to previously reported values in other collagenous soft tissues1,3; however, the range of nanoscale strains exceeds previous estimates1,3. By spatially deconvolving 3D pre-strain maps (Fig. 3), TomoSAXS surpasses previous 2D SAXS studies that have reported only depth-averaged changes. Indeed, owing to the range of fibre orientations and variable tissue-level strain in the IVD, conventional SAXS would have reported an average fibril strain of zero, missing the rich intra-tissue texture and multiscale correlations (Supplementary Note 19). Other soft tissues such as arteries exhibit a multi-layered structure with variable fibre orientation and internal pre-stress; changes in ultrastructural pre-strain at the fibrillar level may also have important biomechanical roles in such systems51,52.

TomoSAXS thus presents a powerful addition to multimodal X-ray imaging for spatial surveys of nanoscale properties53, offering key advantages over approaches such as SAXS-TT28 for the study of fibrous materials (Supplementary Note 20). By spatially registering SAXS data to collagen fibres defined by their 3D orientations (from pCT), TomoSAXS enables fibre-specific—rather than voxel-specific28—assessment of nanostructure. This allows direct analysis of heterogeneous fibre-scattering profiles, with resolution determined by pCT (here 1.6-µm voxel size) rather than the SAXS beam size (here 20 µm; Extended Data Fig. 10), and estimation of fibre-specific nanoscale strain. In addition, TomoSAXS only requires approximately 1% of the theoretical minimum number of SAXS angular projections needed for tomographic reconstruction (Supplementary Note 23).

The combined CT-DVC-SAXS approach is essential to resolve fibril-level strains, with the DVC also providing strain information at the fibre and tissue scales. Tracking fibres across slices allows interpolation methods that preserve fibre continuity. Using the structural model of the fibril-scattering function, rather than the more general spherical harmonic approach, allows more accurate measurements, albeit currently at the cost of increased computational time and greater specificity of the scattering functions for the material investigated. Here the relatively large angular step (22.5°) used for rotations in the rat IVD case (Methods) limited the number of fibres detectable under Ewald conditions to approximately 70%, which can be improved in the future by higher angular resolution (5−10°; Supplementary Fig. 5a). In each horizontal slice around 35–85% of the detectable fibres were solved, which were distributed reasonably uniformly (but not densely) across the tissue volume (Supplementary Fig. 6). To improve spatial resolution, future work may look to improve the SAXS reconstruction pipeline by adding higher-order overlaps to increase the fraction of solvable fibres or adapting alternate global solve strategies.

The reconstruction of fibril properties within an intact human IVD has demonstrated the scalability of the TomoSAXS method; however, challenges arise from the order of magnitude increase in size compared with small-animal models, with 1.5 TB raw HiP-CT data and 800 GB raw SAXS data generated per sample, compared with 42 GB pCT data and approximately 100 GB SAXS data for the small-animal samples tested here. Formalin fixation of the sample will have impacted the nanoscale collagen properties measured here, and future investigation into the effects of fixation should be performed.

Scan time remains a limitation, particularly for the investigation of mechanics in viscoelastic samples, as samples must be stable during scanning (Supplementary Fig. 4). Here the total experimental time for an in situ experiment was approximately 4 h (Extended Data Fig. 1). The need for stress relaxation means that the dynamic response of materials immediately following loading is not captured. Fast (5 s) pCT scan times have been used to capture dynamic loading of cartilage54, and could be combined with the DVC to determine tissue-level and fibre-level strains during loading. Radiation dose is also critical, and its effect on IVD mechanics requires further testing. The total radiation dose applied during in situ experiments was 80.6 kGy (12.2 kGy per SAXS and 26.6 kGy per pCT), compared with approximately 2,000 kGy that would be required to perform SAXS-TT measurements using the same setup. This dose level may have led to a stiffening of collagen fibrils55, but is unlikely to have had a major effect on organ-level or tissue-level mechanics, based on results from previous studies at similar dose levels22,54,56. Total dose for TomoSAXS of human IVD was 15.5 kGy (3.8 kGy SAXS and 11.7 kGy HiP-CT). Although efforts were made to perform physiologically relevant in situ IVD mechanical experiments, truly physiological conditions would require the use of a humidity and temperature-controlled sample environment and multi-axis mechanical testing rig compatible with synchrotron beamlines.

Looking ahead, the TomoSAXS methodology is broadly applicable to other collagenous and soft biological materials, such as tendon3,25 and cornea57, as well as engineered materials. Indeed, experiments on man-made composites would probably have far fewer limitations in terms of viscoelastic effects, hydration and radiation dose. We have demonstrated the feasibility of performing TomoSAXS on intact human IVD, with the potential to extend the technique to other organs including the heart and lungs. Although synchrotron radiation was used here, TomoSAXS could also be undertaken with laboratory X-ray sources at the expense of markedly increased acquisition times. The measurement of fibre orientations from pCT could be replaced with other 3D microscale-imaging techniques, such as optical coherence tomography58. Extending to engineered materials, our 3D diffraction modelling software may also be developed for other periodic and angularly dependent materials including nanostructured polymers7,59 and carbon fibre composites8.

Samples originated from male 8-week-old Sprague Dawley rats kept in controlled conditions (12–12-h light–dark cycles, 22 °C and ad libitum access to food and water) at the University of Manchester Biomedical Sciences Facility. All tissue collection procedures were performed in accordance with the UK Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986, local regulations set by the UK Home Office with institutional approval obtained from the University of Manchester Animal Welfare and Ethics Review Board under the Home Office Licence (#70/8858 or I045CA465). Whole spines were dissected and snap frozen in liquid nitrogen before storage at −80 °C. Thawing and further dissection were performed within 24 h of experimentation, as described by Parmenter et al.22. This resulted in whole IVD samples (from vertebral levels thoracic 10 to lumbar 2; Supplementary Table 1) with half vertebrae on either side. No randomization or blinding was carried out.

Samples were mounted in resin-printed holders (Supplementary Fig. 1) using cyanoacrylate glue (VetBond; 3 M Science), with sample alignment designed so that the mid-transverse slice of the IVD was parallel to the loading plates. A Kapton polyimide tube enclosed each specimen, leaving approximately 0.5 mm exposed. Holders were placed in a Deben CT500 micromechanical tester (100 N loadcell, ±1% accuracy; Deben) with a custom open-frame design22 (Supplementary Fig. 1). Displacement was recorded using a 10-mm extensometer (3-μm resolution, 1% linearity). The open-frame configuration facilitated alignment and hydration of samples while minimizing beam-path obstruction during SAXS. Sample hydration was maintained through immersion in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), supplied via a capillary at the holder base from a 100-ml syringe through a stopped-flow module (Bio-Logic). A continuous flow preserved fluid level despite minor leakage from the 3D-printed holder.

Although simultaneous SAXS and pCT would have been ideal, in the absence of a dedicated SAXS–pCT beamline at Diamond Light Source (DLS), a sequential approach was taken (SAXS(I22) preloaded → pCT(I13) preloaded → pCT(I13) loaded → SAXS(I22) loaded), as illustrated in Extended Data Fig. 1, with special stabilized sample holders and identical mechanical rigs at both beamlines to ensure comparability (Supplementary Fig. 1).

SAXS data were acquired at the I22 beamline of the DLS synchrotron (experiment SM29784-8, 12–15 December 2023). A Deben CT500 was mounted to a rotation stage, on top of the sample table. A Dectris Pilatus P3-2M detector was placed at a distance of 9 m from the stage, with a vacuum tube in between to minimize air scatter. All SAXS measurements used a beam energy of 14 keV and beam size of 20 µm. Each sample was first mapped at 0° angular orientation using a raster map of approximately 100 × 100 SAXS frames using a 50-ms exposure time and a 20-µm step size. Maps were inspected to identify the IVD, and a 5 × 1 mm region of interest was assigned within the IVD for tomographic SAXS scans. SAXS scans were undertaken over raster maps of approximately 250 × 10 SAXS frames with a step size of 20 µm using 150-ms exposure time for nine equally spaced angular orientations (22.5° step) between −85° and 95° (to minimize blocking by mechanical testing support rods). Radiation dose for a full single axis SAXS tomography was 12.2 kGy (Supplementary Note 1). A relatively large step size of 22.5° was used due to a significant reduction in flux caused by the reduced ring current of 200 mA during the beamtime. The experiment can be readily scaled to a smaller angular step (greater fraction of fibres intersecting the Ewald sphere). SAXS data for one horizontal slice is available in the Supplementary Dataset59.

pCT was conducted at the Diamond-Manchester Imaging Branchline I13-2, DLS (experiment SM29784-9, 12–14 December 2023). The setup followed established protocols22 (mean energy of 27.6 keV, 1,800 projections, 0.5-m sample–detector distance), with only the exposure time adjusted to 0.15 s to account for the reduced ring current mentioned in the previous subsection. The insertion device gap was set to 5 mm during scanning and widened to 7 mm for alignment and low-resolution scans to reduce dose. Initial scans used a 1.25× objective (voxel size of 2.6 µm and field of view of 6.7 × 5.6 mm) to capture the sample environment, including the Kapton tube for SAXS co-registration. Subsequent scans used a 2× objective (voxel size of 1.625 µm and field of view of 4.2 × 3.5 mm) before and after compression. Radiation doses were 1.35 kGy (voxel size of 2.6 µm) and 27 kGy (voxel size of 1.625 µm) per scan (Supplementary Note 2). Tomograms were reconstructed using the open source Python library Savu 4.2 (https://savu.readthedocs.io) and further processed using ImageJ 1.54 as previously described22. Images of IVD1 are available in the Supplementary Dataset60.

Samples were held under axial compression, applied in the laboratory vertical z-direction, during scanning. For a reproducible mechanical protocol, two identical Deben CT500 mechanical testing rigs with 100 N load cells were used during the experiment, one placed at beamline I22 (provided by Imperial College London) and the other placed at beamline I13-2 (provided by the University of Manchester at Harwell). A preload of 1 N, corresponding to approximately 40% the animals body weight (260 ± 33 g), was applied at I22 before SAXS scanning to prevent over swelling of the nucleus pulposus (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Samples were allowed 20 min of stress relaxation before scanning to minimize motion, determined as the time taken for load readings to stabilize (less than 0.01-N change in 1 min). Following SAXS, samples were clamped in position using bespoke 3D-printed sample holders and screws (Supplementary Fig. 1) and transferred to I13-2 for pCT (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Clamped samples were placed in the mechanical testing rig at I13-2 and secured at the top (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The bottom platen of the rig was slowly raised until screw hole alignment was reached between the rig and the clamped sample holder, which was then secured in place. The clamps were removed from the sample holder before preload pCT scans. After the first pCT scan at 1.6-µm voxel size, a 50-µm displacement was applied to the bottom platen of the sample holder in the laboratory z-direction, leading to a 2–5% reduction in IVD height (Supplementary Table 1). Axial compression was chosen for ease of experimentation and interpretation of results. Again, samples were given 20 min or more of stress relaxation before scanning. After imaging, the sample was clamped in its loaded state before being removed from the rig and transported back to I22 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). At I22, the sample was placed back in the mechanical testing rig and clamps were removed before taking the loaded SAXS scans, which used the same protocol as described in the section ‘Tomographic SAXS acquisition’ (Extended Data Fig. 1d).

Fibre tracing of the preload 1.6-µm images was performed using the Avizo XFiber module (Avizo 3D 2023.2; Supplementary Fig. 2), with parameters used for tracing given in Supplementary Note 3. After fibre tracing, fibres clearly corresponding to imaging artefacts—such as streaks from mineralized tissues and ring artefacts from reconstruction—were removed from further analysis. Fibre spatial graph data were exported as a .xml file, and fibre identification number was conserved throughout all further analysis.

Fibre orientation and curvature were computed per fibre from a 3D polynomial space-curve fit to the traced fibre centreline4 (r(s)) using a custom-written MATLAB script (MATLAB R2023a, https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs; Supplementary Note 4). This resulted in fibre ID, x, y, z, curvature, α-orientation and β-orientation values for points placed every 6.5 µm along each fibre. Fibre ID, α-values and β-values were converted to 3D volume images for input into the TomoSAXS reconstruction (Supplementary Note 5).

Fibre curvature (k(s)) was evaluated from the first and second derivatives of the fitted curve4 using the standard 3D definition:

A local DVC analysis with flexible point cloud specification was performed using the open-source software iDVC (https://tomographicimaging.github.io/iDVC/)4,21,22,23,24,61. The fibre-based coordinates generated above were used as the DVC point cloud defining the locations of sub-volumes used for tracking (Fig. 2e), resulting in 0.7–1.4 million DVC measurement points per sub-volumes for each sample (Supplementary Table 1). Spherical sub-volumes with a diameter of 40 voxels (65 µm) were matched between the preload and loaded images using a zero-normalized sum-of-square difference function for optimization and 12 degrees of freedom (translation, rotation and first-order strain; Fig. 2g). Six thousand sampling points were placed within each sub-volume for matching. The displacement of the first sub-volume in the point cloud was defined by manually tracking a landmark between the preload and loaded images using ImageJ.

Two strain measurement techniques were applied to the displacement fields measured from the DVC, corresponding to different length-scales probed. For tissue-level strains, the differential of a polynomial fit to the displacement field was used to calculate the Lagrangian strain tensor at each point61. The 75 closest points to the measurement point were used for fitting to smooth out noise in the displacement field and improve accuracy. The first principal strain was derived from the maximum positive eigenvalue, and the third principal strain was derived from the maximum negative eigenvalue of the strain tensor. The direction of the corresponding eigenvectors relative to the local fibre direction was calculated as an angle between 0° (parallel to fibre direction) and 90° (orthogonal to fibre direction; Extended Data Fig. 5g). Radial and circumferential strains were calculated by projecting the strain tensor along the local radial and circumferential directions (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs; Extended Data Fig. 5a and Supplementary Note 6). Fibre strains were calculated using a custom-written MATLAB script (MATLAB 2023a), which performs a polynomial fit to displacement along the fibre direction (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs; Supplementary Fig. 3 and Supplementary Note 7).

The double projection zero strain method22 was used to quantify the accuracy of DVC displacements and strains (Supplementary Note 9). Zero-strain displacement accuracy (mean absolute error) was 88.5 nm and precision (standard deviation of absolute error) was 83.5 nm. Tissue zero-strain accuracy was 0.16% and precision was 0.16%. Fibre zero-strain accuracy was 0.08% and precision was 0.10%. The DVC was able to track a virtual deformation of 10% compression with a displacement accuracy of 198 nm, tissue strain accuracy of 0.40% and fibre strain accuracy of 0.45%.

To calculate orientation for the same fibres in each sample after loading, DVC displacements were applied to the fibre points in MATLAB (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs; Supplementary Note 10). Orientation of the deformed fibres was calculated, and loaded Fibre ID, α and β 3D volume images generated for input into the TomoSAXS reconstruction.

3D diffraction modelling was applied by simulating the meridional X-ray diffraction peaks of collagen fibrils with nanoscale fibre symmetry, under user-defined experimental conditions (wavelength, lattice spacings and angular tilts), and accounting for the variable intersection of the 3D scattering intensity with the Ewald sphere. Implementation was done in a custom Python library developed by us (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs) and is a more complex version of the model presented by Badar et al.1. In brief, the meridional scattering arising from the D-periodicity is simulated by a set of 3D semi-flat ellipsoidal functions, whose location in 3D space is at multiple harmonics of the inverse D-period (q0n = 2πn/D), radial width in q (wa) is related to fibril pre-strain heterogeneity, and angular width (wμ) is related to inverse fibril diameter and intrafibrillar tilting, parameterized by a degree of circularity of the ellipsoid function (δ; 0 = straight function; 1 = circular ellipsoid). The need for a semi-flat, rather than completely flat, meridional ellipsoid came from the experimental observation that even for tissues with uniaxial fibril orientation, the meridional ellipse showed some arcing (Supplementary Note 11). We believe this may be related to the intrafibrillar tilt of the microfibrils38.

Owing to the intersection with the Ewald sphere (radius ∝ 1/λ), the intensity and pattern of the resulting 2D fibril diffraction depends on user-input 3D tilt angles α and β of the fibril, which will be a crucial factor in deciding which fibres contribute to scattering, as well as the beam wavelength. The functions for fibril scattering can be calculated at any point across the diffraction condition of the sphere both in 2D (Fig. 2b, left panel), as well as in 1D (for example, azimuthal (χ) and radial (q) plots; Fig. 2c) by averaging in the complementary axis.

Here the foregoing library (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs), in conjunction with the pCT or DVC data (for α and β), was used to reconstruct the third-order collagen diffraction peak (which typically has intensity between wavevectors of approximately 0.26–0.32 nm−1). The TomoSAXS implementation works via a series of discrete modules in the Python (3.10) environment, summarized here.

Module 1 spatially co-registers the pCT and SAXS scans, from which the individual collagen fibres in each SAXS beam path at all tomographic rotations can be found.

Module 2 performs background correction of the SAXS signals, accounting for PBS, Kapton tube and air scattering, building on the adcorr Python package62. The pCT and co-registered SAXS scans from module 1 allows accurate correction using the variable thickness of the sample through each SAXS beam path by adjusting the proportion of dispersant to sample, compared with assuming a uniform thickness in Pauw et al.62.

Module 3 provides initial estimates for per-fibre SAXS amplitude, using singular-value decomposition (SVD) and the 3D diffraction model.

Module 4—the core of the reconstruction—extracts the nanoscale parameters in an iterative way, by scanning through the SAXS tomography along χ and rotation axes to find angular regions where either a single fibre, a pair of fibres or triplet of fibres dominates the observed scattering over a given angular sector (10° in width). Fibres are isolated at the single, double or triplet level when one, two or a maximum of three fibres contribute predominantly (more than 90%) to total scattering across at least a 10° sector around the circumferential χ axis of individual SAXS frames (Fig. 2c, top panel). By calculating SAXS radial intensity profiles within this azimuthal sector at three equally spaced angular positions (for example, at 0–3.33°, 3.33–6.66° and 6.66–9.99° from the start of a 10° sector), and fitting each radial profile with 3D diffraction models, the parameters mean D-period (inverse to radial peak centre; equation (1)); variation in D-period (peak width along q); and fibril radius (inversely related to peak width along χ) can be estimated. For double-fibre and triple-fibre fits, to avoid degenerate cases where multiple fibres are pointing in the same direction and with similar fibril parameters, we enforced a minimum separation of 5° between fibrils, as well as minimum predicted intensity levels from each fibre to avoid dominance by one (for doublet) or two (for triplet) fibres.

To iteratively solve for the fibre parameters, a two-stage process was followed (Supplementary Fig. 7). First, a sweep was conducted across all rotations and beam paths to isolate and fit single fibres with sufficient independence in scattering intensity across χ, until no more individually isolatable fibres were solvable. The process was then repeated to include fitting for single, double and triple sets of fibres across all beam paths and rotations, looping until no further fibres were solved in a single sweep through all angles and rotations.

Module 5 spatially reconstructs and outputs the estimated metrics and estimates fibril-level (nanoscale) strain in biomechanical loading, using DVC estimates of per-fibre (microscale) deformation to locate the same fibre in the unloaded and loaded datasets.

Spatial co-registration of SAXS and pCT datasets was achieved through identifying fiducial markers (such as the mineralized vertebral endplates) in the samples, which gave distinct signals in SAXS and pCT. The Kapton tube of the sample environment was used for horizontal alignment and the mineralized tissues of the vertebral endplates used for vertical alignment. High-resolution (1.625 µm) pCT images did not capture enough Kapton tube for co-registration, so were spatially registered to low-resolution (2.6 µm) images. Both sets of images were downsampled to a voxel size of 6.5 µm and the offset between them calculated in x, y and z coordinates. Fibre orientation tiff stacks (absolute voxel size of 8.125 µm) were padded to the size of the original high-resolution (1.625 µm) reconstruction (512 × 512 × 432 voxels) and centred using the offset between high-resolution and low-resolution images, so that all pCT data were spatially aligned (Supplementary Note 12).

Vertical registration between SAXS and pCT involved identifying the border of the mineralized vertebral endplates in the SAXS intensity map generated during coarse mapping at 0°, and in the 2D total phase-contrast intensity maps of a sample along the same angular orientation from the pCT data and calculating the vertical offset between them. Horizontal registration was achieved by identifying the Kapton tube from its characteristic peaks in SAXS intensity, and manual segmentation of the tube from the pCT data. For each SAXS tomography orientation (n = 9, −90° to 90°), the fibre orientation, index and Kapton data for vertically isolated SAXS slices were rotated to the corresponding angle (using a custom function for maintaining fibre data integrity during rotation; Supplementary Note 13). The location of the left-hand edge of the Kapton tube was then compared and aligned between the SAXS and pCT data. This allowed finding the indexed fibres that contributed to SAXS scattering along each beam path of the raster scan in the specific SAXS slice. For each frame, the orientation, index and number of CT voxels comprised by each indexed fibre along its beam path were saved, along with the calculated distance between each fibre and the centre of the beam path, which was used as a weighting factor for model fitting. This data were saved as individual matrices, along with the calculated total specimen thickness (along beam path) for each frame.

Background correction was undertaken for each individual SAXS frame following the method outlined in Pauw et al.62. A separate scan using the same parameters as the SAXS tomography was undertaken for a single slice (a slice represents a 1D scan × n = 9 rotations) through (1) an empty Kapton tube, and (2) a Kapton tube filled with PBS, to represent background SAXS signals from both the sample holder (Kapton tube) and the dispersant (PBS). These signals were algorithmically subtracted from each sample SAXS frame using the adcorr Python library (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/adcorr), adjusting the ratio between the sample and dispersant based on the sample thickness for the respective frame (module 1). The resultant background-corrected data were saved as .h5 files for each TomoSAXS slice.

The first analytical step in the TomoSAXS algorithm makes an initial estimate of the amplitude of SAXS scattering for individual fibres using the SVD, using a mean value for the other peak characteristics such as position, radial and angular widths (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Note 14). This was justified by the small variability of the peak position (from 2D data) across different sample locations. The estimation step was used to identify locations of strong scattering for specific fibres enabling fibre-by-fibre solution in the next module 4 step.

At a given beam path in the sample x, and a rotation angle r, the angular intensity of the third-order collagen peak q0 can be written as

where the sum in i is taken over all fibres in the volume, with weighting factors either 0 (if outside of the beam path) or proportional to the intensity at the fibre location (assuming a Gaussian beam profile with known shape). As all fibres are taken to have the same average peak location and width parameters in this initial estimation step, the contribution from each fibre \({I}_{i}^{r}(\chi ;{q}_{0},\Delta {q}_{0},\alpha ,\beta )\) can be calculated up to a scaling factor proportional to the amplitude factor Ai, including the geometrical transformations needed to account for fibre orientation with respect to the beam. Hence, when represented for each \(x,\chi ,r\) the above equation can be expanded into an overdetermined set of linear equations, which can be solved by SVD.

A Python dictionary was created with entries for each SAXS frame comprising of 0–180° intensity(χ) (herein I(χ)) radial integrations between 0.26 and 0.32 nm−1 in q, binned to 36 averaged points across χ and smoothed using 1D Savitzky–Golay filtering (window length of 9 and polynomial order of 1). Two matrices were then created: the first consisting of a single vector comprising the concatenated I(χ) integrations for all SAXS frames (left-hand side (LHS) in the equation above); and the second with columns comprising the contribution of each fibre to the same binned I(χ) intervals predicted for each SAXS frame using 3D diffraction modelling (right-hand side (RHS) in the equation above). The amplitude for each fibre was then estimated by non-negative linear least squares regression, regressing predicted versus measured I(χ) data. A Python dictionary was constructed, with entries for each indexed fibre consisting of its index, α and β angles and an empty entry for fitted nanoscale parameters. This dictionary was used to calibrate registration matrices (see above) for each rotation angle of the SAXS tomography, creating a series of other dictionaries.

As shown in Fig. 2f–h, TomoSAXS reconstruction was based on fitting fibre diffraction models of intensity to measure I(q) profiles across the azimuthal angular ranges (Fig. 2g) of independent scattering signals from either (1) a single fibre, (2) a pair, or (3) a triplet of overlapping fibres (Supplementary Table 2). We first calculate simulated angular SAXS intensity profiles using estimated amplitudes from module 4. A Python fibre dictionary was constructed, containing its index, α and β angles, initial estimated scattering amplitude and a dictionary for fitted nanoscale parameters. The dictionary was referenced against registration matrices (see above, module 1) for each rotation angle of the SAXS tomography, creating a series of individual orientation-specific dictionaries, indexed by beam path.

For each beam path in the orientation-specific dictionary, a dictionary indexed by fibre index stored information for every fibre in the beam path (including initial estimated amplitude), with a weighting term from the calculated distance of the fibre to the beam centre (Supplementary Note 13) where d is the distance from the beam centre and w the beam diameter:

These dictionaries were used to create simulations of the angular scattering intensity of the third-order meridional peak of every beam path using 3D diffraction modelling, using tilt angles obtained from pCT and the averaged nanoscale peak metrics (q0 = 0.2856 nm−1, wa = 0.005 nm−1, wµ = 0.2 nm−1 and δ = 0.5; see Supplementary Note 14 for rationale).

The angular intensity profile was scanned to iteratively solve individual or small groups of fibres, rather than fitting all fibres to the data, simultaneously (Supplementary Note 16).

Single-fibre fit. For each fibre k in a beam path p at a rotation r, its individual angular intensity contribution \({I}_{k}^{p}(\chi ;{r})\) to the total intensity \({I}^{p}(\chi ;{r})\) was calculated. If the following condition was fulfilled for an angular range \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) between 0 and 2π (Δχ = 10°), and a single-fibre dominance threshold ts = 0.90:

then the fibre k was identified as being the dominant contribution to the SAXS signal in the \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) angular range. The index, beam-path location and angularly independent sector \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) was recorded for all fibres that met the user-defined criteria for independent scattering were stored in a Python list.

Next, these fibres were fitted to extract the nanoscale (fibrillar) peak metrics, by calculating \({n}_{\chi ,c}\) (default = 3) equally spaced radial slices (azimuthally integrated) across the \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta ]\) angular region, with a width \(\Delta {\chi }_{c}\) (default = 6°). These were simultaneously fitted with 3D diffraction models for the fibre, using the minimize() function of the lmfit Python library (https://lmfit.github.io/lmfit-py/fitting.html) and the Nelder–Mead algorithm. The angles α and β and the weighting factor of the fibre were fixed parameters, and q0, wa, wμ, amplitude and δ were set as fit parameters (see Supplementary Table 2 for settings and Supplementary Note 15 for rationale). If the fits passed several quality thresholds, both relating to absolute values of the parameters and statistical quality of fit (for standard error, threshold = 25%), the fit values were added to the dictionary entry for the respective fibre. Instances in which the fit to the fibre did not meet quality thresholds were saved and added to a separate Python list allowing them to be discarded from future investigation. This process was repeated for all the fibres in the list.

As successful fits allowed more potential single-fibre instances to be identified (already fitted fibres could be deconvolved from the scattering in all beam paths where they occur), the process was repeated until no more instances of independent scatter for single fibres could be found for any beam paths in the SAXS tomography.

The above process isolated and fitted the instances with the strongest independent scattering signal (approximately 10–20% of indexed fibres per slice), providing robust fits for further deconvolution and fitting of other fibres occurring in the next step of the reconstruction algorithm.

Overlapping fibre fit. In the next step, the reconstruction algorithm included fitting of instances where two to three fibres produced a combined scattering that meets the thresholds for independent scatter. For example, for all pairs of fibres \({k}_{1},{k}_{2}\) in the beam path \(p\), we checked whether the following condition was fulfilled for any \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) and a double-fibre dominance threshold td = 0.95:

For multiple-fibre fits, validation simulations (Supplementary Note 15) have shown that the dominance of one fibre’s scattering intensity can bias the fit of the other fibre (or fibres) and lead to inaccuracies in fits. Hence, upon identification of a pair of fibres \({k}_{1},{k}_{2}\), the relative combination of scatter from each fibre was estimated. Only instances in which each fibre represented a minimum of \({t}_{d}^{1},{t}_{d}^{2}\) = 20% of the total scatter across > 90% (0.90) of the angular sector \([{\chi }_{k;1}^{p},{\chi }_{k;1}^{p}+\Delta \chi ]\) were considered for fitting. Instances that passed this test were then fitted using the minimize() function as above.

After each fit, the parameter database was updated, and each angular intensity profile was scanned to identify any new solvable fibres (single, double or triple), which could be fitted by deconvolving already fitted fibres.

The foregoing steps were looped through all beam paths at all rotations, for a user-defined maximum number nl = 10 times, recording the ratio of fitted versus total indexed fibres at the end of each loop. If no increase in fitted fibres was observed at the end of a loop, the loop was terminated as all possible fibres had been fitted.

The entire TomoSAXS pipeline was conducted on a per-slice basis (per-horizontal 20-µm SAXS tomography slice) using cluster computing (specifically the DLS computing cluster). This allowed each slice to be run in parallel to maximize efficiency. The complete process across each of the five modules was completed within 6–7 days, with each module triggered individually in an iterative manner. TomoSAXS fitting (4–5 days) resulted in a mean proportion of fitted fibres of 60.08% per slice. This included multiple fits for differing instances of individual fibres found within different TomoSAXS slices. It is important to note that this does not correspond to the proportion of the total sample represented in each slice being fitted, as TomoSAXS operates on a per-fibre basis as opposed to a per-voxel basis (as in SAXS-TT28). Reconstructions are spatially heterogeneous and dependent on the density and orientation of fibres within the respective slice.

Once fitting was complete, fitted parameters were spatially reconstructed for scanned fibres to create volumetric maps of per-fibre values. This was performed per slice for each parameter, by creating blank maps of the same shape as fibre index maps (created during the registration process; Supplementary Note 13) and assigning metric values to the voxels assigned to the index of every solved fibre in index maps. For fibres with fitted values in multiple TomoSAXS slices, if slices remained unfitted between these points, they were provided with values between fitted values estimated using linear interpolation.

To estimate strain in nanoscale parameters under compressive load, indexed fibres were isolated that provided fits in both unloaded and loaded data. For each unloaded fit, the estimated vertical deformation of this point (and thus position in the loaded TomoSAXS scan) was estimated using the vertical (z axis) deformation measurements provided by DVC analysis (Supplementary Note 17). Strain in each parameter was calculated as the percentage difference between unloaded and loaded TomoSAXS fits for each point.

The spatial calibration between pCT and SAXS data allowed estimation of the accuracy of fits supplied by the TomoSAXS technique, by providing known artificial nanoscale parameters to each indexed fibre in each TomoSAXS slice (maintaining fibre orientation, initial estimated scattering amplitude and per-instance weighting; Supplementary Note 18). Experimental noise was added to the simulated SAXS data, and accuracy and precision of nanoscale parameter estimates calculated as mean absolute error and standard deviation of absolute error.

Chicken foot tendons were dissected and air cured under differing tare loads of 0.5 N, 1.5 N and 3.5 N to generate different levels of pre-strain in the collagen. Three tendons were arranged at different overlapping orientations and superglued to a 3D-printed sample holder (Extended Data Fig. 2a). SAXS scans were performed using a Xenocs Xeuss 3.0 (DLS) with a beam size of 400 µm and exposure time of 5 min. Nine angular rotations between 0° and 180° were used, with 11 beam paths per rotation. µCT of the sample was performed using a Phoenix V|tome|x (Research Complex at Harwell) with a voxel size of 14.3 µm.

The orientation of collagen fibrils within each tendon was assumed to be aligned with the principal axis of the tendon. The sample was divided into an 11 × 11 grid for TomoSAXS reconstruction rather than individual fibres, for the purpose of a simplified, proof-of-concept reconstruction (Extended Data Fig. 2). TomoSAXS reconstruction followed modules 4 and 5 of our pipeline, with no background correction or SVD analysis of scattering amplitude applied.

Static imaging of a whole, formalin-fixed, human IVD (spinal level thoracic 11–12, 64-year-old male donor, no known spinal pathologies) was performed at the BM18 beamline of the ESRF using hierarchical pCT45 (Supplementary Note 21). Donation and dissection were performed at the Laboratoire d’Anatomie des Alpes Françaises in November 2023, in accordance with French legislation governing body donation. Subsequent transport and imaging protocols were approved by the UK Health Research Authority through the Integrated Research Application System (#200429) and the French Ministry of Health.

The entire IVD was captured with a voxel size of 10 µm and a local zoom with a voxel size of 4 µm performed centrally to enable clear visualization of collagen fibres throughout the complete organ (Fig. 4b,d). Fibre tracing was performed on the 10-µm scan using the Avizo XFiber module (Avizo 3D 2023.2), with parameters used for tracing given in Supplementary Note 21. Correlative high-energy (75 keV, beam size of 100 µm) tomographic SAXS was performed at ESRF beamline ID31 at 24 angles (Supplementary Note 22).

TomoSAXS reconstruction of a single slice of human IVD followed a modified pipeline to overcome the increased number of angular rotations, the 103 increase in sample volume and concomitant increase in fibre density per beam path. In principal, this involved three primary modifications. First, α and β fibre-angle maps were independently quantized by k-means clustering of non-zero angles rounded to 3° increments, then combined pixel-wise into a 3D orientation label map of unique vertical–horizontal fibre pairs, reducing fibre indices from more than 26,000 to approximately 3,600. Second, we extended the multiple-fibre fitting strategy to include four-fibre and five-fibre clusters across the angular χ axis. Finally, to handle the larger number of beam paths and greater amount of indexed objects per beam path, we introduced parallel processing. Instead of running rotations sequentially, each rotation was processed in parallel on a computing cluster, with all rotations reading from and updating a shared database of fitted fibres so that they could inform one another during execution. For more details of these modifications, see Supplementary Note 22.

Two-sided ordinary least squares regression analysis was used to test the agreement of known versus estimated properties of digital phantom data with and without the addition of experimental noise (Extended Data Table 1). Correlations between per-fibre mean values of fibre strain, D-period, D-period variation and D-period strain were tested using ordinary least squares regression (Extended Data Table 2). No adjustments were made for multiple comparisons.

An example dataset (rat IVD) is available (https://doi.org/10.5522/04/30286255), with all the data required to run TomoSAXS reconstruction for a single slice. Any supplementary information in this study is available in the paper and the Supplementary Information. Additional data are available from the corresponding authors upon request.

All code created for this project is available in a dedicated GitHub library (https://github.com/DiamondLightSource/tomosaxs).

#1326. Sarri: ‘Atalanta conceded a stupid goal, but with 14 players out, we take the point’

Maurizio Sarri insists Atalanta ‘will take the point’ against Kairat Almaty, despite ‘conceding a stupid goal,’ and hope to secure Conference League qualification ‘when we have more of our squad available.’

La Dea badly needed a victory to boost morale as well as their standing in the Conference League after a win over Pafos and 2-0 defeat away to Ajax, but it was only a meagre point at home against Kazakh side Kairat Almaty.

They had gone behind to a classic counter-attack from Marc Gual, but managed to claw back an equaliser with substitute Nikola Krstovic.

“If you have 14 players out at the same time, and you consider this a week to relaunch the season, that seems tough,” Sarri told Sky Sport Italia.

“We had 10 players injured today, plus four who the medical staff told us should not be used for more than 30 minutes. We certainly could’ve won tonight if we hadn’t conceded a stupid goal, then it became an uphill struggle.

“Fortunately we didn’t give up, so we tried to the end to bring home a positive result. It was a struggle, we moved the ball around too slowly and failed to find spaces in a very defensive opponent.

“With so many difficulties that we were dealing with, we take the point and hope to secure qualification later in the tournament, when we have more of our squad available.”

Atalanta have not won any of their last seven matches between Serie A and the Conference League, and went into a three-day training retreat after Monday’s humiliating 3-0 home defeat to Parma.

Considering the side that Sarri put out this evening, did he expect better from his players?

“One always expects a lot from his players. Gianluca Scamacca was injured, so I only saw him train for the first time yesterday, so it’s hard to expect much more from him right now.

“Undoubtedly, I expected more from a few players, but we are in a period where we’re playing eight games in 23 days and forced to do it with the same limited group.”

It was always going to be difficult for Sarri to get Atalanta to adapt to his very different style of football after more than a decade in the Gian Piero Gasperini vein, but the injury crisis has slowed that process further.

“Clearly, this is a big transformation, and then if we have added difficulties like this… Tonight we played two defenders from the Under-23 team who only really have experience in Serie C, plus Kamaldeen Sulemana who got hurt on August 2 and has only been back with the team for four or five days.

“It’s also tough because none of the players have history with me, so what was already a complex process has had new layers of difficulty put on top.”

need to sa k.this chain smoker its not working for atlanta

It’s not working as there is no settled team at the moment for Atalanta, with 10 players out and 4 who can only play 30 minutes that is a huge dent in to team cohesion. Having a bunch of youth players in the side gets them blooded and looks like there are real talents in there (Obric and Idele look quality but need experience). Not only that, in the last few games they have been hit on the counter after dominating the first halves. Though a comeback to a point is a positive.

have to stop with this nonsense excuse about injuries. They had close to 10 players that play for their international teams currently on the field today…you can’t beat a Kazakh team with that? come on

Liverpool and Chelsea are reportedly among the biggest suitors for the transfer of RB Leipzig centre-back Castello Lukeba.

Other top clubs such as Manchester United and Barcelona have also been mentioned as teams keeping a close eye on Lukeba’s situation at Leipzig, as per journalist Ekrem Konur.

We’ve previously seen Lukeba linked with big moves, with Man Utd also mentioned as having pursued him in the summer, when Football Transfers reported that he had an €80m release clause.

Now there’s been another update as Ekrem Konur has posted on X about clubs circling for Lukeba in what could end up being a major transfer battle for the Frenchman…

? #RBLeipzig RB Leipzig centre-back Castello Lukeba has emerged as one of the top defensive targets for several European giants.

? Liverpool, Chelsea, Manchester United, Bayern Munich and Barcelona are all reportedly considering the French defender as a priority option for… https://t.co/RxziVGd9gZ pic.twitter.com/H8qKJFureZ

— Ekrem KONUR (@Ekremkonur) November 6, 2026

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

“RB Leipzig centre-back Castello Lukeba has emerged as one of the top defensive targets for several European giants,” the Turkish journalist posted. “Liverpool, Chelsea, Manchester United, Bayern Munich and Barcelona are all reportedly considering the French defender as a priority option for their backlines.

“Lukeba’s athleticism, ball-playing ability and long-term potential continue to attract strong interest from across Europe. A major battle for Castello Lukeba’s signature could develop in the upcoming transfer windows.”

It will be interesting to see how this pans out, as Lukeba looks like he could certainly be a strong signing for the likes of Chelsea and Liverpool.

Both of those clubs could do with bringing in a new centre-back, and we’ve been made aware of AC Milan’s Koni De Winter also being of interest, as reported exclusively via the Daily Briefing earlier today.

Lukeba is another option who’d surely help LFC as they look for a long-term replacement for the ageing Virgil van Dijk, while CFC look in need of upgrades on inconsistent performers like Wesley Fofana in their backline, while summer signing Maxence Lacroix has also had a mixed start and is now injured.

It seems inevitable that Lukeba will leave Leipzig at some point, with the Bundesliga side often tending to cash in on their star names at some point, and usually for a significant profit.

The 23-year-old should now be approaching his peak years, and he’ll surely be keen to represent a bigger club and perhaps test himself in the Premier League.

#1324. CELTIC RATINGS: Star turns emerge from the bench to save the day but how many of Martin O'Neill's starting XI earned pass marks? Very few...

Published: 18:29 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:30 EDT, 5 November 2026

Substitutes Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran sparked Celtic into life as the Scottish champions got off the mark in the Europa League in a 3-2 victory over Besiktas.

Martin O’Neill’s side were heading for a seventh defeat in 11 matches and bottom place when Junior Olaitan netted on the rebound after Sam Johnstone had saved his 54th-minute penalty.

But Osmand drilled home the equaliser with his first touch in the 62nd minute, seconds after coming off the bench in a triple change, and the 20-year-old set up Duran to put the hosts in front.

Besiktas sub Orkun Kokcu equalised from long range but Celtic went back in front within 60 seconds when Duran stabbed home an 87th-minute winner from six yards.

The win hands Celtic a fighting chance of progressing, with Portuguese second-tier side Torreense as their next opponents. But who caught the eye last night and who flattered to deceive on what turned into a long-overdue glory night at Celtic Park?

Sebastian Tounekti competes with Emirhan Topcu but in truth he had another shocker overall

Besiktas’ opener came from a bad kick-out. He does not look convincing with the ball at his feet and was lacking at the leveller.

Looks like a guy who hardly ever plays, but there are absolutely no excuses for the moronic tackle on Poka that gave away a spot-kick.

Really strong at the back before going off and did so much to repel a Besiktas side that couldn’t make their possession pay.

Made some individual errors in the first half but forced a great save with a header and generally did his job defensively.

Did his bit in what was a decent defensive display before the subs came on and changed it. Also involved in the winner.

Benjamin Nygren tries his luck but it was another underwhelming evening for the big Swede

Good pass to Osmand for the goal, but no one escapes criticism for a horrific first hour. Could he also have closed down Kokcu?

Improved as the game developed after an underwhelming first hour or so. Won some decent balls in midfield as Celtic prospered.

Forced a save with Celtic’s first shot on target on 50 minutes and earns some credit for that, but offered very little else before going off.

Wasted a great chance when blazing high and wide on seven minutes and just doesn’t offer enough regularly enough.

When is there going to be an acceptance that this guy isn’t up to the mark? Offered next to nothing before making way for Osmand.

Kasper Hogh cuts a desperate figure as he troops off at half-time on another blank evening

A jigsaw piece that has just made its way into the wrong box. Duran came on late on and changed everything. He’s the main man.

SUBSTITUTES: Callum Osmand (Tounekti 61), Colby Donovan (Lotomba 61), Camilo Duran (Forrest 61), Haissem Hassan (Hogh 78), Dane Murray (Carter-Vickers 78).

Inspired subs? Hardly. His starting XI suggested Europe is not his priority. Just like his board. And that really isn’t acceptable.

BESIKTAS (4-2-3-1): Nubel; Murillo, Agbadou (Djalo 70), Topcu, Ouattara (Yilmaz 83); Olaitan, Salih Ozcan (Kokcu 76); Cerny (Fakili 83), Trossard, Poku; Oh (Vlahovic 70).

#1323. UEL | AZ Alkmaar 1-2 Juventus: Special K success in Alkmaar

Juventus secured an impressive 2-1 win away to AZ Alkmaar, who were unbeaten at home in Europe for over three years, as Teun Koopmeiners and Randal Kolo Muani kept strong Europa League form going.

The Bianconeri had a much-needed 2-0 victory over Napoli on Sunday and were unbeaten in the Europa League with two wins and a 2-2 draw against Rennes. Injuries continued to pile up, as Weston McKennie joined Kenan Yildiz, Manuel Locatelli, Nico Gonzalez, Francisco Conceicao, Zeki Celik, Khephren Thuram and Kamil Grabara on the treatment table, so Jeff Ekhator was added to the UEFA list.

Teun Koopmeiners faced his younger brother Peer, with both coming up through the AZ youth academy, and the crowd had a pre-match banner depicting them as children. The Dutch side lost the opening Europa League fixture at Sunderland, then beat Hapoel Beer Sheva and Ararat-Armenia, but were unbeaten in 17 UEFA home fixtures stretching back to October 2023.

Jeroen Zoet, Jizz Hornkamp, Wouter Goes and Stije Resink were out of action, but Kees Smit was back in the squad for the first time since September 20. They lost their last two Eredivisie games without finding the net.

Randal Kolo Muani’s angled drive flashed across the face of goal to skim the far post, and the ex-PSG man was instrumental in the opening goal.

Kolo Muani flicked the ball up over a defender to get down the right and pulled back to the edge of the area, where Teun Koopmeiners was ready to sweep in with the inside of the left boot. The midfielder did not celebrate against his hometown club, with his brother captaining them.

Things went from bad to worse for the hosts, who were forced into a change for the Lewis Schouten injury moments later.

Kerim Alajbegovic’s scorcher skimmed the crossbar at the far top corner from just inside the box, but AZ Alkmaar started to push back, Guglielmo Vicario right behind the deflected Dave Kwakman strike.

Juventus doubled their lead when a high Kolo Muani press forced Mees de Wit into an error, Nick Woltemade returning the pass for the Frenchman to bend the left-foot finish into the far bottom corner.

Alajbegovic hesitated when Teun Koopmeiners intercepted a mistaken Jari De Busser pass and the chance went begging, then Federico Gatti sprinted from his own half only to over-hit the final ball for Kolo Muani.

Smit came off the bench and saw his effort charged down by Lloyd Kelly, then fired another very promising attempt over from 12 yards while the hosts had penalty appeals rejected when Elijah Dijkstra went down under pressure from Kelly.

AZ Alkmaar did eventually get back into the game when Ayoub Oufkir robbed Kelly at the touchline and sent Dijkstra down the right, pulling back for Mexx Meerdink to tap in from close range.

Suddenly the hosts were fired up and had the ball in the net again during added time, but Meerdink was offside when his header forced an extraordinary Guglielmo Vicario save, so the rebound from Mees de Wit did not count.

The pressure was on to the final whistle, including a Smit free kick into the crowd that could’ve gone anywhere, but Juve held on.

T Koopmeiners 19 (J), Kolo Muani 37 (J), Meerdink 88 (A)

#1322. Martin O'Neill tells Celtic to keep believing they can reach Europa League knockouts after stirring revival

Published: 18:27 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 18:45 EDT, 5 November 2026

Martin O’Neill urged his Celtic side to focus on making it to the knockout stage of the Europa League after a second-half comeback against Besiktas that reminded him of the glory days against the continent’s elite at Parkhead.

The Premiership champions ran out 3-2 winners thanks to a dramatic 87th-minute clincher from two-goal substitute Camilo Duran and racked up their first points of the campaign to put themselves into 32nd place in the league phase table.

Celtic were a goal down to a Junior Olaitan effort on the rebound after a saved penalty when Duran, Callum Osmand and Colby Donovan were thrown on just after the hour and changed everything.

Osmand levelled with his first touch before Duran put Celtic ahead on 78 minutes. And after Orkun Kokcu had made it 2-2 in the 85th minute with a low drive, Duran popped up three minutes from time to complete a chaotic and badly needed victory.

Manager O’Neill confessed the atmosphere reminded him of his first spell in charge at the turn of the millennium when he led his side to famous wins over the likes of Juventus and Porto and took them to the UEFA Cup final in 2003.

Now, he has ordered his players to concentrate on at least making it into the top 24 of the Europa League and securing a play-off spot.

O'Neill punches the air with delight as his team savour first win in Europa League group

‘I was delighted with the performance,’ said O’Neill. ‘It was fantastic. We put our heart and soul into the game and played some really decent stuff, particularly in the second half.

‘Just when we thought we were going to drop two points, we came roaring back again to win. It was a magnificent effort by the team. So much spirit and heart and desire to go and claw their way not just into the game, but through it.

‘There was a bit of nervousness because we hadn’t a point on the board, but it had everything. We rose to the occasion tonight and what we’ve done is that we’ve given ourselves a chance. We always still think about trying to qualify.

‘Mostly, the crowd give us something and tonight was particularly special. A European night again and it reminded me of the olden days.’

O’Neill also defended his decision to leave Duran, Osmand, Donovan and Haissem Hassan out of the side in favour of the likes of Sebastian Tounekti, struggling record signing Kasper Hogh and Jordan Lotomba, who gifted the penalty-kick that gave Besiktas the lead early in the second period.

Duran , second from left, is hailed by team-mates after scoring winner against Besiktas

‘Lotomba had his first start for us and you are trying to find out as much as you can about players,’ said O’Neill. ‘I made some changes to the side to freshen things up knowing that some of the players — for instance, James Forrest, who was magnificent for us — might not last the game.

‘We had to give the opportunity because we have played a lot of games in relatively quick succession and we go again on Sunday.’

Osmand made a quickfire impression when smashing in a terrific goal from distance after taking a pass from Callum McGregor and has challenged his team-mates to keep delivering the kind of display that turned the game round in the last half-hour.

‘It caught me off guard. I know Cal is good at that reverse (pass) and I am just so glad I caught it nicely,’ said the talented 20-year-old.

‘In my head, I was all jittery and just wanted to come and do something. I want to make something happen and I am so happy with tonight.

A smiling Duran savours the acclaim of Celtic fans after giving the team a 2-1 lead

Osmand helped turn the game around after scoring equaliser with his first touch

‘We did really well to go and win the game. This is what we try to do. The place was rocking at the end and we need to keep bringing these sort of performances and doing well.

‘We have it in us. We have just got to try and keep doing it.’

Osmand also reserved special praise for Colombian hitman Duran in the wake of his matchwinning display.

‘Camilo did amazing. He is such a poacher and scores amazing ones and then poaching ones, so all credit to him,’ he stated.

‘I think the team dug in really well at the start. We stayed strong and got our rewards finally.’

Swedish attacker Benjamin Nygren believes that getting the Europa League campaign back under their own control is hugely important ahead of Celtic’s final four fixtures.

‘We fought very hard and earned the three points in the end. We fought well during the whole game and created enough chances to score more goals,’ said Nygren.

‘This was a very important game and we have it in our own hands with four games to go.

‘We go into every game to win it and we earned it today against a good opponent. We need to continue like this.’
