#1302. Sir Alex Ferguson Named the Greatest Player in Premier League History

Rob is senior football editor at GiveMeSport, with over 15 years experience covering sport in various capacities since graduating from the University of Gloucestershire in 2008 with a degree in journalism. A childhood obsession for all things football developed into a career writing about the beautiful game, initially producing content for clients including Luton Town Football Club and the PGMOL. His first big interviews were with Premier League referees Howard Webb and Michael Oliver in 2009. He then spent four years producing written content for a betting website, mainly focusing on football, and was there to cover various games and tournaments including the 2010 World Cup and Euro 2012. Rob joined GiveMeSport in 2013 (initially as a sub-editor before becoming a senior writer and then senior editor in 2020) and has covered countless football matches and other sporting events, interviewed various high-profile figures including Rio Ferdinand, Peter Crouch and Theo Walcott, and written well over 10,000 articles during that time. Rob has played a key role in GiveMeSport's coverage of the World Cups in 2014, 2018 and 2022, plus Euro 2016, Euro 2020 and Euro 2024, along with many Champions League finals. While football is Rob's area of expertise, he has also covered a wide range of other sports during his time at GiveMeSport including boxing, tennis and darts, as well as the 2016, 2020 and 2024 Olympic Games.

Sir Alex Ferguson, regarded by many as the greatest football manager of all time, once named the player he believes is the best in Premier League history.

Twenty-four former players have been inducted into the Premier League’s Hall of Fame since its creation in 2021.

The Premier League’s all-time leading goalscorer Alan Shearer and Arsenal legend Thierry Henry were the first two players inducted, followed by Roy Keane, Frank Lampard, Dennis Bergkamp, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham.

Others are certainties to be inducted, such as Cristiano Ronaldo, one of the greatest footballers in history, who scored 103 goals for Manchester United and won the Premier League Player of the Season award in 2007 and 2008.

Fellow shoe-ins include Mohamed Salah (193 Premier League goals) and Harry Kane (213 Premier League goals).

However, only players who are officially retired from professional football are eligible to be inducted into the Premier League’s Hall of Fame.

One player conspicuous by his absence is Ryan Giggs, winner of more Premier League titles (13) than any player in history.

Only James Milner (658) and Gareth Barry (653) made more Premier League appearances than Ryan Giggs (632), who also boasts the highest number of Premier League assists (162) by a distance.

No official explanation has been given for Giggs’ continued omission, although BBC Sport noted in January 2025 that many have concluded ‘the controversy over his character lay behind his absence’.

Asked by his former Manchester United teammate whether it plays on his mind, Giggs said: “Not really. No, I mean, I don't think about it until you just brought it up. I don't think about it. I think when you start off, you don't... These are the things that you're not striving for. You're striving off to win games and try and win trophies. That's the most important thing for me.”

There’s little doubt that Ferguson would have inducted Giggs into the Hall of Fame if it were down to him.

Ferguson named Giggs as one of only four genuinely world-class footballers he managed at Manchester United, and even labelled the Welshman as the best player in Premier League history back in 2009 - five years before Giggs retired aged 40.

"We have had a lot of top-class players in this league – and some have probably made more of an impact than Ryan – but nobody can boast the same sort of longevity and consistency," Ferguson said of Giggs, per The Guardian.

"He was there when the league started and he is still there now. I think you would have to say Ryan is the best."

While some lean towards the likes of Henry, Ronaldo or Shearer among the greatest Premier League players of all time, the greatest manager in Premier League history believes Giggs’ remarkable longevity and consistency puts him in pole position.

#1301. 'Winning at the Emirates is very hard... but we were a team of warriors': Hull City hero GEOVANNI on his iconic goal against Arsenal, why it very nearly never happened and why the Tigers 'will always be in my heart'

Published: 21:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

The greatest moment in Hull City's Premier League history began with Geovanni trying to go home.

'I was ill all night, I barely slept at all,' says Geovanni, who was gripped by a fever and thumping headache less than 24 hours before he was due to walk out at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium in September 2008. The Brazilian rang his wife from the team hotel to tell her he was coming home and planned to have someone pick him up.

Thankfully, his wife Roberta would not hear of it.

'God really used her that day,' he tells Daily Mail Sport. 'She said: "Geovanni, stay there, God will honour you. Hang on and tomorrow try to get a bit of sleep."'

When Hull staff came to his room the next morning, he asked to be left to sleep. He dosed up on medicine and went for lunch, but sat out the light pre-match training session with his temperature touching 38 degrees Celsius.

'And then I got to that game, which was so spectacular,' he says, 'and I was able to score and help Hull beat Arsenal.'

Geovanni unleashes a spectacular equaliser for Hull at the Emirates Stadium back in September 2008

The goal inspired a famous comeback win for the Tigers, who became only the second team to win away at Arsenal

It was Hull's first league meeting with Arsenal for 93 years, in the first top-flight season of the club's then 104-year history.

Arsene Wenger's side had started the day top of the table and Paul McShane's own goal put Arsenal ahead after 51 minutes. Most expected the floodgates to open.

But 11 minutes later up stepped Hull's brilliant Brazilian, a marquee signing from Manchester City in the summer of 2008 after the Tigers' unexpected promotion.

Geovanni cut inside Theo Walcott and sent a 25-yard rocket into Manuel Almunia's top corner. Daniel Cousin headed in a historic winner four minutes later and Hull became only the second side to beat Arsenal at the Emirates.

'Beating Arsenal at the Emirates is very hard, and we pulled it off,' says Geovanni, now 46, speaking from his home in Brazil. 'That was a team of warriors, great players, and we had a really good friendship. And that day we walked away with a great win.'

On Saturday, Hull return to the Emirates to face the champions and league leaders. The Tigers are 11th after nine games. It is a strong start that few predicted.

'Hull have to give 100 per cent, the maximum, be switched on the whole time,' says Geovanni. 'It's difficult, but it's not impossible, because Hull really did beat Arsenal.'

Eight days after the Emirates match, Geovanni did it again. A stunning 30-yard free-kick at White Hart Lane nestled into the top corner past his friend and compatriot Heurelho Gomes.

'We beat Tottenham with Gareth Bale, Luka Modric, all those players,' he says. 'For me, those two are top-drawer. They're two great players who left a mark on me.'

The win moved Hull into third and by the end of October they were level on points at the top. 'London 0 Hull 2' read the headline in the local paper, in reference to Hull band The Housemartins' 1986 album London 0 Hull 4, as the city revelled in its newfound fame.

Geovanni (centre) was part of another iconic Premier League moment, when Phil Brown gave his team a public dressing down at half-time of a loss at Manchester City

The Brazilian returned to Hull's MKM Stadium last year and received a hero's welcome

Geovanni took centre stage. Arriving on a free that summer after being released by Manchester City, he credits manager Phil Brown and assistant Brian Horton for giving him a second chance in the Premier League.

'They were very special people in allowing me to stay in England, which was my dream,' he says. 'And I learned a lot from both of them. Brian was a very experienced coach, he played for Hull, he managed there, so the affection and respect are huge. Whenever I can talk about them, I do.

'In the first year, Hull surprised a lot of people precisely because of the way we played. Sometimes we'd start in a 4-3-1-2, I played as the No10 behind two strikers. And if we were struggling to mark, I'd drop in to close down the left flank and we'd go back to a 4-4-2.'

The dressing room did the rest. Richard Garcia, an Australian winger with Uruguayan parents, helped translate team talks from English into Spanish and captain Ian Ashbee, Nicky Barmby and Bernard Mendy all made Geovanni feel welcome. 'I'm really happy about the friendships I made in that dressing room,' he says.

Geovanni was part of another of the Premier League's most iconic moments, when he and his team-mates received a public dressing down from his manager on the pitch at half-time of a 5-1 loss to Manchester City on Boxing Day 2008. Eleven months later, Jimmy Bullard scored a penalty before recreating the telling off in celebration.

'It was good for breaking the ice,' says Geovanni. 'From that day on the atmosphere got better too, because we can all make mistakes. The most important thing is to admit the mistake and move on.'

Geovanni's finest moment for Manchester City, with whom he spent one season after stints with Barcelona, Benfica and Cruzeiro, came in the Manchester derby, where he was called into the side by manager Sven-Goran Eriksson because Stephen Ireland was ill.

'He called me over and said, "Geovanni, this game... are you ready?". That was the best news I'd had all day, knowing I was going to start.' The day did, in fact, get better. Geovanni scored the only goal in a 1-0 victory.

Geovanni smashes home a winner for City in the Manchester derby, a year before his move to Hull

United were a familiar victim. In December 2005, his diving header for Benfica helped knock Sir Alex Ferguson's side out of the Champions League in the group stages

He struck again against United in November 2008, in a 4-3 defeat for Hull at Old Trafford

United were a familiar victim. In December 2005, his diving header for Benfica helped knock Sir Alex Ferguson's side out of the Champions League in the group stages, while he also scored in a 4-3 defeat for Hull at Old Trafford in 2008.

'A player has to turn up in the big games,' he says. 'United were a machine back then: Giggs, Paul Scholes, Gary Neville, Anderson, Ronaldo, Rooney.'

Geovanni's greatest regret, though, remains that he didn't heed the advice of Barca boss Louis van Gaal, who wanted to turn the wannabe striker into a wing-back.

He reflects: 'If I could go back in time, I'd listen to what Van Gaal said, because it would have been easier for me to fight for a place at wing-back than as a striker, where there were great players: Javier Saviola, Rivaldo, Patrick Kluivert, Marc Overmars.'

Luiz Felipe Scolari, his coach at Cruzeiro, gave him his only senior Brazil cap, against Mexico at the 2001 Copa America. 'It was a dream for me: to leave a town of 4,000 people (Acaiaca) and one day represent Brazil,' he says. 'He (Scolari) was a father to me.'

These days Geovanni is a volunteer pastor in Belo Horizonte and runs a players' agency with his father-in-law and an old youth-team friend.

But Hull will always be in his heart. He has a picture of himself in a Hull shirt in his house and received a hero's return after heading back to the city last year.

'I love them (the fans). I have a very special affection for the Hull supporters,' he says. 'It was two years in which I gave everything. I went back there last year and was really well received, it was great: friends from my time there, the fans too.

Battling Blackburn's Damien Duff in a pre-season friendly in his Barcelona days. He spent only two seasons with the Catalan club, having left Cruzeiro to move to Europe

'I'm very grateful for everything they did for me. Hull and the fans will always be in my heart'

'And I know I left my mark on the club's history. Whenever people talk about Hull City, about Brazilians, they'll remember Geovanni, the time I spent there, the feats we achieved together.

'And I believe I gave those fans a lot of joy, in games that seemed impossible. God blessed me and I was able to score goals and bring joy to that city. I'm very grateful for everything they did for me. Hull and the fans will always be in my heart.

'My two years at Hull were perhaps the two most special years for me. The sweetest spell of my career.'

#1299. 25 Best Defenders in World Football Right Now (Ranked)

A strong defender is vitally important to any successful football team. Sorting out the back-line is crucial, and having some serious defensive talent is a surefire way to build a team destined for silverware. Much focus is placed on attacking players, which is why any list of the best footballers in the world will always be dominated by that type of star.

However, we've highlighted the best defenders in the world right now, in order to give them their flowers for a change. From buccaneering full-backs to commanding centre-halves, the beautiful game is laced with talented defenders in all shapes and sizes. Here are the best players who operate at the back in a role that has been unsung for too long.

Given that trying to separate those on the list is such a difficult task, a number of factors will be taken into consideration as to where they end up in the rankings. These include:

The imposing France international is a great example of the modern centre back: athletic, composed, and complete with impressive attributes that exceed his defensive capabilities. Dayot Upamecano built a formidable duo alongside Ibrahima Konaté at RB Leipzig, leading both to the French national team and transfers to elite European teams.

Upamecano has established himself as a key part of Bayern Munich's defensive setup, securing several league titles and domestic cup triumphs since his move in 2021. With France, Upamecano has featured regularly, winning the Nations League in 2021 and playing the entire 120 minutes of France's World Cup final loss to Argentina in 2022. In 2026, he was one of nine defenders to be nominated for the Ballon d'Or.

Luka Vuskovic has been a revelation since joining Brighton & Hove Albion in the summer of 2026. The Croatian has been tipped for great things since a loan spell at Hamburg put him on the Seagulls' radar in the first place. Tottenham Hotspur still decided to sell up, however, cashing in for as much as £50m.

Known for his aerial ability, recovery pace and modern passing range, the young defender is already among the very best in his position. The future is certainly bright.

Marc Guehi has been a fine defender for a number of years now but has really established himself at the highest level over the past three seasons.

He performed well for England at Euro 2024, as they made it to the final of the tournament, losing to Spain. He then followed that up by captaining Crystal Palace to their first-ever major trophy, as they defeated Liverpool in the FA Cup final, before beating them again to win the Community Shield a few months later.

Guehi earned a big move to Manchester City in 2026 after a 2025 summer move to Liverpool fell through. The England man has since established himself at the heart of the defence, helping the club to win the FA Cup during the 2025/26 season.

Alphonso Davies has been one of the most exciting attacking fullbacks in football for some time now, really breaking into the Bayern Munich team during the 2019/20 season, in which he helped deliver a treble – made up of the Champions League, Bundesliga and the DFB-Pokal.

In total, he has seven league titles under his belt in Germany and has enjoyed a great deal of success with Bayern. The only issue has been fitness problems, as injuries have regularly interrupted his momentum in Munich. Davies will hope to keep himself fit if he wants to move higher up this list.

Riccardo Calafiori has quickly become one of the best defenders in the world. Swapping centre-back for a fullback role at Arsenal, the Italian has often provided a surprise goalscoring threat, combining his instinct inside one area with his defensive prowess in the other. He is among the most undroppable players under Mikel Arteta.

Injuries have threatened to delay his progress, but Calafiori still played a key role as Arsenal finally ended their wait for another Premier League title in the 2025/26 campaign.

While AC Milan are counting their lucky stars that they took a punt on Theo Hernandez’s signature in the summer of 2019, it’s his previous employers, Real Madrid, who will be kicking themselves for letting him go for such a paltry fee. Since moving from Spain to Italy, most fans would agree that Hernandez consistently ranks among the world's best defenders every season.

From Essien to Kaka, here are the 10 greatest players who have played for Real Madrid and AC Milan.

Quick enough to burst forward with ease, while his high IQ allows him to marshal the back line from the left-back berth, the Frenchman has every tool to play at the top level of the sport for the next decade or so. However, a recent move to Al-Hilal may make it difficult for him to keep his place in this list without regularly playing in Europe.

Marc Cucurella has undergone what many would consider to be somewhat of a redemption arc in the last couple of years. At Brighton, he was lauded as one of the best left-backs in the Premier League before his 2022 move to Chelsea led to a decline in form as he came close to being kicked out of Stamford Bridge within a year of his arrival.

What seemed to catapult him back into better form was Spain’s Euro 2024 victory. From that point, the full-back regained his confidence and mojo and, as a result, became an incredibly valuable member of both Chelsea and Spain's squads. After winning the 2026 World Cup with Spain, Cucurella earned a huge move to Real Madrid during the 2026 summer transfer window.

Over the course of the last 24 months, Willian Pacho has transitioned from a young defender looking to show his worth in European football to a winner of the continent’s biggest competition and one of its most highly touted defenders.

The Ecuadorian, who made a name for himself in Belgium and Germany before his big-money move to the French capital in 2024, has settled in at the Stade de France incredibly well. Linking up with the likes of veteran Marquinhos, he has excelled thus far as part of the back-to-back Champions League-winning squad. The future continues to look bright for Pacho.

When Abdukodir Khusanov's header allowed Chelsea to open the scoring just three minutes into his Manchester City debut, many predicted that it would be the defining moment of his Man City career for all the wrong reasons. Since then, however, he has been among the best defenders in the world.

The young centre-back is among the quickest in his position in the Premier League, if not the world, and uses that recovery pace to his advantage. Despite his age and relatively small stature, Khusanov also has no trouble when asked to outmatch opposition forwards on a physical level - winning 60% of his duels in the 2025/26 campaign.

There were some doubts over Ezri Konsa's ability to step up for a side like Arsenal. Those doubts couldn't have been put to bed any quicker if he tried, however.

The England defender has taken a seat at the top table and has not looked back since, having also won the Europa League with Aston Villa in the 2025/26 campaign. At the start of the 2026/27 season, he ensured that the Gunners didn't miss William Saliba during his absence for a single second.

It's worth noting that Konsa is also an England mainstay these days. The centre-back has earned his place for the Three Lions and could be crucial if they are to finally end their wai for silverware.

#1298. Extra Champions League Spot: Still a long-shot for Italy despite improved ranking

An extra spot in next season’s Champions League is still looking like a long-shot for Italy despite moving up in the latest UEFA rankings after the latest round of European fixtures played this week.

The latest round of European fixtures saw Inter beat Feyenoord 3-0 away from home in the Champions League, Roma lost 3-2 away against Manchester United, Como smashed Lens 9-1 in an historic scoreline whilst Napoli lost 4-1 away against Porto. In the Europa League, Juventus claimed a 2-1 victory over AZ Alkmaar, but Milan fell to a 2-0 defeat at home against Ferencvaros. Atalanta were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Kairat in the Conference League.

It was a mixed set of results for the Italian sides competing in Europe this week, but these results were still enough for Italy to move one place up in the UEFA season association coefficient, which is used to determine the two nations that are awarded an extra Champions League spot in next year’s competition.

Italy began the week in ninth place in the UEFA season association coefficient, and have since moved up to eighth place in the rankings after the latest update on Thursday night.

Italy’s overall score has also improved from 6.500 to 7.500 after the latest round of European results.

As things stand, England sit at the top of the rankings with a score of 9.166, Portugal are in second with 8.900, Belgium in third on 8.400, Germany in fourth with 8.285, Turkiye in fifth with 7.900, Spain are sixth with 7.875 and the Netherlands are in seventh with 7.666.

Italy, along with England, Spain and Germany, are among the nations whose leagues are guaranteed four places in the Champions League, but there is also a chance of a fifth being added.

Two nations are awarded an extra Champions League spot each, known as the European Performance Spot, which went to England and Spain for the 2025-26 and 2026-27 tournaments. Italy and Germany received the extra Champions League spots in 2024-25, the first edition of the tournament after its expansion to 36 teams.

The European Performance Spot is awarded to the two nations that finish the previous season at the top of the UEFA Season Association Coefficient.

In this system, nations are awarded points based on the performances of their teams competing in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League.

Each team is awarded two points for a victory, one point for a draw and zero for a defeat. Those points are halves for qualifying and play-off matches. Clubs are also awarded bonus points depending on their positions at the end of the league phases, and extra points for each round they progress through after that.

Those scores are added up and divided by the number of clubs a nation has competing in UEFA competitions that season.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1297. Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The dynamics of isolated quantum systems following a sudden quench has a central role in many areas of material science, high-energy physics and quantum chemistry1,2,3,4. Such far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics—which features complex phenomena with implications for thermalization, non-equilibrium phase transitions and Floquet phase engineering5,6,7,8—is challenging to study numerically, in particular, in high-dimensional systems9,10. Here we use a programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator11 to systematically explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits. By initializing the system in a product state and performing quenches across a broad parameter space, we discover several stable, qualitatively distinct dynamical regimes. We trace their robustness to Floquet-like prethermal steady states8 that are stabilized over exponentially long emergent timescales by strong dynamical constraints. We further observe sharp peaks in the dynamical response that are quantitatively explained by the structured melting of prethermalization through resonances. In two dimensions, we uncover a prethermally driven, first-order dynamical phase transition linked to the proliferation of Néel-order defects6,12, and probe it quantitatively using a generalized Clausius–Clapeyron test. Together, these results establish a programmable route to high-energy prethermal phase structure: long-lived dynamical phases, their resonant breakdown and a first-order dynamical phase transition that is not inherited from the equilibrium phase boundaries.

Numerical simulations for a 1D chain of N = 16 atoms with periodic boundary conditions and Rb/a = 1.4. a,b. Simulations including the full experimentally relevant noise model. a. Time evolution of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) at Δ/Ω = 0.2 and 3.7. Solid curves show noisy numerics including readout confusion; shaded regions indicate the total 1σ uncertainty obtained by combining trajectory and shot-noise errors in quadrature. Noiseless numerics and experimental data are shown for comparison. b. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning, averaged over 0≤t≤4 μs; shading indicates the corresponding total 1σ uncertainty. The noisy numerics use the Aquila-relevant noise model of Extended Data Table 1, with 20 stochastic trajectories, 120 shots per time point, and a sampling interval of 0.01 μs. c,d. Simulations including only positional atom disorder. c. Increase of the resonance peak width near Δ/Ω ≈ 3.7, relative to the zero-disorder case, as a function of the positional disorder strength σp, extracted from Lorentzian fits, together with a simple classical estimate. d. Time-averaged \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) versus detuning for several values of σp. Increasing positional disorder selectively broadens and smooths the resonance peaks, while leaving the rest of the long-time response comparatively unchanged under experimentally relevant noise.

Experimental results for 180 atoms on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. a. The time-averaged expectation values of several k-island observables, namely the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable for k = 1, 2, 3, over time intervals with (top) different initial times ti and fixed final time tf = 4.0 μs, and (bottom) fixed initial time ti = 0.8 μs and different final times tf. The grey dashed vertical lines mark the quench parameters of the time series in panel b, namely the peaks of each island operator (Δ/Ω = 0.0, 1.2, 3.6, 4.8) and the point close to the right exit of the xy 1-island operator region (Δ/Ω = 2.0). b. The time evolution of the expectation values of the xyd 1-island observable and the xy k-island observable with k = 1, 2, 3. The drawing on the right shows an example of island conversion processes possible in the 2D system (equivalent to the 1D island conversion Hamiltonian discussed in the Supplementary Information). The arrows in the panels indicate the time series segments for the main resonance at Δ/Ω = 3.6 that tentatively reveal island conversion dynamics: two-islands are rapidly created and then slowly converted into a mix of one- and three-islands. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The time-averaged expectation values of the island operator sum on the cut Rb/a = 1.4 for 16 atoms, and the thermal expectation values of the observable for the effective temperature of the quench using the nearest-neighbor blockade subspace (thermal xy blockade) and the full Hilbert space (thermal full). b. The dependence of the time-averaged blockade violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(1)}\) (also shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a) on V1/Ω at representative constant detuning cuts for 144 atoms. To normalize the blockade violation density to the connectivity and boundary conditions, we scale it by N/NB, where NB = 2NxNy − Nx − Ny is the number of nearest-neighbor bonds. The states along these cuts are prethermal, and thus over a fixed time interval the time averages after peak exhibit exponential scaling [equation (22)], as evidenced by the dashed lines showing fits \(\propto {e}^{-c({V}_{1}/\varOmega )}\). As shown in the Supplementary Information, the upward curvature observed in the experiments relative to the clean exponential scalings at large V1/Ω can be explained by the position disorder, while the calibrated readout errors set the final saturation floor. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

a. The dependence of Δc/Ω (as extracted from \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{L}^{(1)}\rangle }\) using the procedure described in Methods) on inverse linear system size for Rb/a = 1.4 cut. The classical prediction, given by Δc/V2 = 2 − 2(1/Nx + 1/Ny) + 2/(NxNy), is shown for comparison. b. The dependence of the conjugate variable jump ratio (\({\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}\rangle }/{\delta }_{c}\overline{\langle {\sum }_{i}{\hat{n}}_{i}{\hat{n}}_{\langle \langle i\rangle \rangle }\rangle }\)) on the inverse linear system size. The jump ratio is used to probe the Clausius-Clapeyron relation at the DPT. Both the transition point and the jump ratio converge as the system size increases, consistent with a first-order transition. The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting statistical and fitting uncertainties as described in Methods.

The classical spin dynamics model is described in the Supplementary Information, where the 2D square lattice has coordination numbers z1 = z2 = z3 = 4. a. Dynamical phase diagram in terms of the long-time averages of the (squared) spin component \({S}_{z}^{2}\). Panels b,c show the three (squared) spin components on b. the cut Rb/a = 1.4 across the phase transition and c. the cut Rb/a = 0.7 across the crossover, each indicated by a grey dashed horizontal line in panel a. The black dashed lines in panels a,b show the phase transition from the approximate analytic solution of the Stoner-Wohlfarth model.

Experimental phase diagrams extended down to Rb/a = 1.0 for 144 atoms. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the Rydberg density observable \({\hat{O}}_{n}\) and the k-neighbor correlation observables \({\hat{O}}_{nn}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2 (defined in the main text). Besides the crossover, at low Rb and Δ ≈ 2V1 we observe another distinct dynamical regime, which corresponds to antiblockade dynamics73 characterized by expanding excitation loops74. b. The time-averaged expectation values of the xyk-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3 (equation (4) and surrounding text). The atom schematics in the upper corners show the types and sizes of Rydberg excitations that the observables measure. The grey horizontal line indicates the lower bound Rb/a = 1.2 of the phase diagrams for 180 atoms shown in Fig. 4a. The first-order DPT smooths to a crossover at low Rb, in analogy with the classical Stoner-Wohlfarth scenario (Extended Data Fig. 5). The experimental data shown are derived from 100 samples per time evolution, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

The lattices are shown for Rb/a = 1.4. 1D lattice with a. 52 atoms; and b. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 2 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. 2D square lattice with c. 180 atoms; and d. 16 atoms, where the field of view can accommodate 6 parallel copies with separation b = 5a. e. Pulse sequences. (Top) The Rabi frequency Ω is set to a constant value Ω/2π = 2.5 MHz. (Bottom) The detuning Δ is set in the range Δ/Ω ∈ [−4.0, 6.0], and shown here for Δ/Ω = 0.4.

Experimental results on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. Panels a-c show experiments with (left) N = 52 atoms and (right) N = 16 atoms. The geometries are shown in Extended Data Fig. 7. a. The time-averaged expectation values of the \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) observables and the k-island observables \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) for k = 1, 2, 3. Experimental \({\hat{O}}_{L}^{(k)}\) data is equivalent to Fig. 3b. b. The time evolution of the expectation value of the 1-island observable for several values of Δ/Ω on the right exit from the central region, shown as dotted vertical lines in a. c. The time-average \(\bar{p}(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega )=\frac{1}{T}{\sum }_{i}p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,{t}_{i})\) of the Hamming weight probability distribution \(p(\alpha | \varDelta /\varOmega ,t)={\rm{Tr}}\,(\rho (t){\hat{P}}_{\alpha })\). Projectors \({\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\) arise from the spectral decomposition of the (unnormalized) Hamming weight operator \({\hat{Q}}_{n}\equiv N{\hat{O}}_{n}={\sum }_{\alpha }{\lambda }_{\alpha }{\hat{P}}_{\alpha }\), where λα = 0, …, N denote the possible Hamming weights. The time average is equivalent to marginalization over ti with p(ti) = 1/T. The grey dashed vertical lines identify the distribution at Δ/Ω = 0. d. The mean and variance of the time-averaged Hamming weight probability distribution at Δ/Ω = 0, measured in experiments with different system sizes N. The data are linear, with fits yielding the slope of ~0.275 ± 0.002 for the mean and ~0.106 ± 0.006 for the variance, shown respectively by the red and green solid lines. The approximate scalings are 1/4 and 1/8, shown respectively by the red and green dashed lines, consistent with a state that ergodically explores the blockade subspace. e. The time-averaged Hamming weight probability from numerical simulations with 16 atoms. The experimental data shown are derived from 120 samples per time evolution for 52 atom experiments and 100 samples per time evolution for 16 atom experiments, with error bars denoting one standard deviation across the samples.

Numerical studies of multiple observables, scaling, and averaging for the 1D chain in a circular geometry on the cut Rb/a = 1.4. The time-averaged expectation values are computed as \(\overline{\langle \hat{O}\rangle }=\frac{1}{{t}_{f}}{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{f}}{\rm{d}}t\langle \hat{O}(t)\rangle \). a. The time averages of the blockade-violation density \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) operator, the diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\) operator (also presented in the main text Fig. 2d), and the off-diagonal \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) operator. The \({\hat{O}}_{nn}\) response vanishes at the main peak, but captures the resonances, suggesting their origin from blockade violations; the \({\hat{O}}_{XX}\) response showcases non-analyticities at points where the dynamics is expected to change abruptly. b. The time averages for different system sizes N = 10, …, 20 and final time tf = 10 μs. The curves are nearly identical, indicating a weak system size dependence. c. The time averages for N = 16 atoms and different final times tf. The curves rapidly converge in tf ≈ 0.5 μs. The dashed line denotes the curve for tf = 100 μs, which is the longest time examined in the numerics, while the squares denote the diagonal ensemble averages, which are equal to the time averages in the strictly infinite-time limit. d. The time averages of the blockade-violation operator for N = 16 atoms and different quench parameters Δ/Ω, reflecting the 1D experiments in Fig. 3a. Similar to the experimental results, the curves show exponential decay, corroborating prethermal dynamics even at small system sizes.

Numerical results obtained using the time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) method for a chain of N = 52 Rydberg atoms with open boundary conditions. The blockade radius is Rb/a = 1.4. The system is evolved up to \({t}_{\max }=4.0\,\mu {\rm{s}}\) with a time step Δt = 0.01 μs, and the Hamiltonian includes nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions, with longer-range terms truncated. a. Real-time dynamics of \(\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle \) for two representative detunings, (top) Δ/Ω = 0.0 and (bottom) Δ/Ω = 0.5, illustrating convergence of the oscillatory behavior with increasing maximum MPS bond dimension \({\chi }_{\max }\). b. Time-averaged value \(\overline{\langle {\hat{O}}_{ZZ}\rangle }\) as a function of detuning Δ/Ω, where the plotted values are averaged over the final 2.0 μs of the evolution. The curves correspond to different maximum bond dimensions \({\chi }_{\max }\). Both the real-time dynamics and the time-averaged observables exhibit rapid convergence as \({\chi }_{\max }\) increases, with \({\chi }_{\max }\gtrsim 256\) yielding nearly indistinguishable results, indicating that the dynamics are well converged with respect to entanglement truncation at the probed times.

#1296. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

England manager Thomas Tuchel has revealed that Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall came extremely close to earning his first senior international call-up, praising his performances and explaining where he sees the 28-year-old fitting into his system.

Dewsbury-Hall has enjoyed an impressive spell at Everton, establishing himself as an important player and continuing to push for international recognition.

Despite his performances, the former Chelsea and Leicester City midfielder was left out of Tuchel’s latest England squad for the upcoming internationals against Croatia and Spain.

His Everton teammate James Garner, however, was included once again, raising questions about how far Dewsbury-Hall remains from receiving his first senior opportunity.

Speaking at Wembley on Friday, Tuchel was asked by GIVEMESPORT reporter Sam Cohen about Dewsbury-Hall’s omission, particularly given his performances for Everton and previous involvement in England’s provisional squads.

The German was full of praise for the midfielder and admitted that he had been seriously considered for selection.

“Very good player, very good season, you can just see it,” Tuchel said.

“He’s a very good football player overall because I see him in the way we play now.

“I don’t see him in central midfield in the build-up and in the build-up of the game. I see him more in the finishing part of the game as an offensive eight or almost as a 10.”

Tuchel’s assessment offers an interesting insight into how England’s coaching staff view Dewsbury-Hall’s qualities.

Rather than considering him primarily as a deeper midfielder responsible for progressing possession, the England boss believes his strengths are better suited to operating further forward, where he can influence attacks in the final third.

However, that is also an area of the pitch where England have considerable competition for places.

“The competition is very, very high in our squad in this position,” Tuchel continued.

“But he is, as you know, he’s in our 55, a standout player for Everton and we see his quality.

He’s a nice watch because he’s a very, very good football player and was very, very close for me.

Those comments will offer encouragement to Dewsbury-Hall, who has previously spoken about being included in England’s provisional squads without making the final selection.

While Garner’s inclusion demonstrates that Tuchel is keeping a close eye on Everton, Dewsbury-Hall faces a different challenge because of the attacking midfield role the England manager believes suits him best.

Crucially, Tuchel’s comments suggest the midfielder is not being overlooked entirely.

Instead, he remains firmly within England’s wider selection picture, with his performances at club level continuing to attract attention.

For Dewsbury-Hall, the task now is to maintain his form and convince Tuchel that he deserves an opportunity in one of the most competitive areas of the England squad.

Grealish will NOT be involved in Everton’s next Premier League fixture either.

#1294. The Ins and Outs of Mancini’s latest Italy squad: 11 dropped, 8 new additions

Roberto Mancini named an Italy national team squad of 31 players on Thursday evening ahead of November’s Nations League fixtures against France and Belgium, but who dropped out and who are the new additions to the latest Azzurri squad?

Italy will be in action against France in San Siro next Thursday, November 12, and away against Belgium on Sunday, November 15.

As things stand, Italy sit in second place in their Nations League group on seven points after four matches. France lead the way on 10, Belgium are in third on six and Turkiye are bottom on zero.

After naming a squad of 34 players for his first camp back in charge of the Italy national team last month, Mancini has named a roster of 31 players this time around. 11 players that were named in Mancini’s squad back in September have dropped out and eight new faces have been called in.

Some of the players that have dropped out of the squad have returned to the U21s, where they will be more likely to gain playing time this break, including goalkeeper Massimo Pessina, defender Eddy Kouadio and striker Samuele Inacio.

Injuries have ruled Giovanni Di Lorenzo, Giacomo Raspadori and Moise Kean out of selection this time around.

The other names to drop out of the squad are Bryan Cristante, Rolando Mandragora, Daniel Maldini and Mohamed Ali Zoma.

As for the new additions, there is a return to the squad for Marco Palestra, who has recently made his first Premier League appearances with Chelsea after picking up an injury a few days before the season kicked off.

Niccolo Pisilli has returned, as has Samuele Ricci. The Como midfielder was not originally named in Mancini’s 34-man squad when it was announced in September, but was later called in as a replacement for Cristante, who left the camp through injury.

Completing the new additions are Alphadjo Cisse, Mattia Liberali, Luca Koleosho, Riccardo Cassano and Simone Lontani.

17-year-old Cassano and 18-year-old Lontani will be with the senior squad for a few days to train and effectively audition in front of Mancini, but will then return to the U18 and U19 squads later on in the week, where they will be more likely to earn minutes this break.

Out: Massimo Pessina (Bologna), Diego Coppola (Brighton), Giovanni Di Lorenzo (Napoli), Eddy Kouadio (Monza), Bryan Cristante (Roma), Rolando Mandragora (Torino), Samuele Inacio (Borussia Dortmund), Moise Kean (Como), Daniel Maldini (Cagliari), Giacomo Raspadori (Atalanta), Mohamed Ali Zoma (Nurnberg).

In: Marco Palestra (Chelsea), Riccardo Cassano (Como), Niccolo Pisilli (Roma), Samuele Ricci (Como), Simone Lontani (Parma), Alphadjo Cisse (Milan), Luca Koleosho (Paris FC), Mattia Liberali (Como).

Goalkeepers: Marco Carnesecchi (Atalanta), Gianluigi Donnarumma (Man City), Guglielmo Vicario (Juventus).

Defenders: Honest Ahanor (Crystal Palace), Alessandro Bastoni (Inter), Riccardo Calafiori (Arsenal), Federico Dimarco (Inter), Daniele Ghilardi (Roma), Michael Kayode (Brentford), Gianluca Mancini (Roma), Marco Palestra (Chelesa), Giorgio Scalvini (Atalanta).

Midfielders: Nicolò Barella (Inter), Riccardo Cassano (Como), Issa Doumbia (Sporting CP), Nicolò Fagioli (Fiorentina), Davide Frattesi (Lazio), Simone Lontani (Parma), Niccolò Pisilli (Roma), Samuele Ricci (Como), Alessandro Romano (Cagliari), Sandro Tonali (Tottenham).

#1292. How James McAtee became Nottingham Forest's tough-tackling 'quarterback': The heart-to-heart with Oliver Glasner, summer boot camp and an Adam Wharton blueprint

Published: 21:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

Quarterback is not a word necessarily associated with somebody once dubbed the 'Salford Silva' but then James McAtee has changed immeasurably since leaving Manchester City 15 months ago.

That moniker was handed down when the diminutive midfielder was much younger, effortlessly gliding through City’s academy, excelling in tight spaces, never losing possession. Scoring heaps, too.

That is who Nottingham Forest thought they were purchasing for £30million in August 2025, a statement signing to play high up the pitch. And yet as last season unravelled, and the sackings piled up – four managers in all – McAtee mustered only two Premier League starts throughout the campaign.

He was given four minutes across almost four months at one stage and was an unused substitute in both encounters with City. That will change on Saturday, McAtee one of the first names on the Forest team sheet, owing much to one conversation with Oliver Glasner that changed the course of his career at the City Ground.

So to the quarterback. The most important position in a Glasner team. That was how the Austrian envisioned McAtee’s evolution, the path to regular matches, and within months he has become the heartbeat of a team that is deserving of significantly more points than the six they have amassed so far.

Those who oversaw McAtee's development at City are not shocked by the calm use of possession and incisive passes through the lines yet did not predict him flying into challenges and blocks, only two midfielders in the division having completed more tackles than his 14 so far. He has turned into a terrier.

James McAtee in his 'quarterback' role for Nottingham Forest, where he has become the heartbeat of the team

At Manchester City he was dubbed the 'Salford Silva' and was more effective higher up the pitch

This has been a product of a full summer’s work on a rented pitch in Stockport, close to the family home. Forest's sporting director George Syrianos had made it clear that McAtee needed to become more physically robust and, after a five-day holiday, he spent a regimented two-and-a-half hours a day training, including 60-minute weight sessions in the afternoons.

When he arrived back for pre-season, McAtee had put on just over 2.5kg of muscle and lost 1kg of fat. He turned up a new man and that served to rubber stamp Glasner’s idea of permanently moving him into the engine room.

The Forest boss spoke to the 24-year-old about how he had developed Adam Wharton at Crystal Palace into an England international and that the plan here would be exactly the same.

This month’s Nations League ties will come too soon for that yet there are those within the FA who are confirmed admirers of McAtee and expect him to earn future caps. That he skippered the Under 21s to last year’s European Championship title, was player of the match in the final against Germany and named in the team of the tournament holds real weight inside St George’s Park.

Aesthetically, he is the picture of what the FA have wanted to create over the past decade: a nimble yet tough midfielder who guards the football with his life and wriggles out of trouble without fuss. And whose game understanding means he knows when to force the issue – McAtee has created the same number of chances as Rayan Cherki (18) this season.

The only central midfielders to have attempted more passes into the box than McAtee’s 60 are Bruno Fernandes, Granit Xhaka and Pascal Gross.

City will be some test on Saturday evening and there is plenty for him to prove, having worked under Enzo Maresca with the club’s Under 21s and a lingering feeling of what might have been at the Etihad Stadium.

As for England, they are blessed with real quality coming through in central midfield, with Alex Scott at Bournemouth leading the charge to unsettle the axis of Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice.

Scott could return from a thigh injury sustained during the last international break this weekend, a fitness problem that enraged his club.

McAtee skippered the England Under 21s to last year’s European Championship title, was player of the match in the final against Germany and named in the team of the tournament

The 24-year-old bulked up over the summer and is now able to mix it in the Forest engine room

Beyond those three it is very much up for grabs. James Garner is a recent Thomas Tuchel favourite, largely owing to his work ethic, with Wharton overlooked for the World Cup.

The man picked ahead of all those, Manchester United’s Kobbie Mainoo, was not afforded a kick in the United States. McAtee’s defensive and offensive stats this season outstrip the others in that chasing pack. They all know that there is definitely a claim to stake for somebody.

It’s Rice, Anderson, Scott and another at this point. Whether McAtee can kick on beyond nine consecutive Premier League starts is up to him. Crucially, he is in control of his own destiny more than ever before.

At City, he patiently waited for chances that barely came. In his debut year at Forest, players considered safer bets jumped the queue as the club battled relegation. But under Glasner, he has been harnessed, given the assurances that one sub-par performance does not mean a spell on the bench. McAtee has always been somebody who needs love to flourish and has finally found some.

#1291. Four players earn first call-ups in latest Italy squad: Everything you need to know

Four players earned their first senior national team call-ups when Roberto Mancini announced his squad of 31 Italy players for November’s Nations League fixtures against France and Belgium, plus another who is set to earn their first ‘proper’ taste of international action: Here is everything you need to know about the fresh faces in the latest Azzurri squad.

Italy will be in action against France in San Siro next Thursday, November 12, and away against Belgium on Sunday, November 15.

As things stand, Italy sit in second place in their Nations League group on seven points after four matches. France lead the way on 10, Belgium are in third on six and Turkiye are bottom on zero.

Ahead of the November round of fixtures, Mancini announced a squad of 31 players on Thursday evening, which included first call-ups for 17-year-old Como midfielder Riccardo Cassano, Parma 18-year-old Simone Lontani, Milan top scorer Alphadjo Cisse and recent Champions League goalscorer Mattia Liberali.

There was also a call-up for Luca Koleosho, who earned his first two caps in a pair of friendlies under interim head coach Silvio Baldini back in June, as part of a squad that was made up almost entirely of players from the U21 squad. This is his first call-up to a competitive camp.

The most surprising inclusion on the list is 17-year-old Cassano, who has not yet made a competitive appearance at club level.

The talented teenager, who likes to play in front of the defence, capable of dictating and breaking up play, was only promoted to Como’s U21 squad at the beginning of the season and earned his first call-up to the U18s squad in September.

He travelled, trained and earned minutes with the senior Como side during pre-season, but is yet to appear competitively under Cesc Fabregas. His appearances this season have all come in the Primavera league or in the UEFA Youth League.

Cassano will spend the first few days of the international break with the senior Italy squad and will have an opportunity to impress in front of Mancini, but will then be released back to the Italy U18s squad, where he is more likely to earn match minutes this break.

Like Cassano, 18-year-old Parma forward Lontani will also spend the first few days of the international break with the senior Italy squad before returning to the Italy U19s to earn game time at the right age group.

The teenager, who came through the academies of Cesena and Milan, joined Parma over the summer and has gone on to score five goals from his first 11 senior appearances at club level, including three in 10 outings in Serie A.

Lontani’s appearances so far this season have largely come as a second striker, but he is capable of covering in a number of central positions as well as on the left wing if required.

It was only a matter of time before Cisse was included in the Italy squad: There had been calls for him to be included back in September as well. The 20-year-old, in his first season, is currently Milan’s leading goalscorer across all competitions with seven from 12 appearances.

He brings a level of versatility to the Italy attack, capable of playing as a striker, in a supporting role behind the centre-forward or as a left winger.

Unlike Cassano or Lontani, Cisse will be targeting his first minutes for the senior Italy side during the November round of fixtures.

Fresh off scoring his first Champions League goal in Como’s historic 9-1 drubbing of Lens earlier this week, Liberali will have an opportunity to prove his worth with the Italy squad this month.

The 19-year-old is not quite a regular in the Como line-up just yet, but is beginning to earn opportunities off the bench under Cesc Fabregas. He current has two goals and two assists from six appearances across all competitions so far this season, three of those goal

Involvements were in the 9-1 victory over Lens on Wednesday night.

He and Cisse know each other well given that they both spent the 2025-26 season in Serie B with Catanzaro.

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1290. In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1,2,3,4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1–SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5,6,7,8,9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1–SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

a, Quantification of CD3− cells 5 days after CRISPR-mediated gene editing in three independent donors. b, Quantification of live cells 5 days after editing with the indicated Cas9 mRNA concentrations, n = 3 biologically independent replicates. Data are shown as mean + s.e.m. Significance was calculated using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test. ns, not significant. c, Left, representative flow cytometry plots showing CD3 and CD28 protein-level DKO efficiency in activated human primary T cells 5 days after Cas9 mRNA electroporation. Right, quantification of CD3+ CD28+ cells in DKO and vector control groups; data are shown as mean + s.e.m.; n = 4 infection replicates. Significance was calculated using a paired two-sided t-test, ****P < 0.0001. d, Quantification of CD3− or CD28− cells 5 days after editing; n = 3 donors per concentration. Data are shown as mean ± s.e.m. e, Classification and composition of targeted genes in the T cell DKO CRISPR library. f, Schematic of the two-step T cell DKO CRISPR library construction process. g, Quantification of plasmid library sgRNA-pair construct distribution. h, Flow cytometry histograms showing EGFRvIII expression in U87-GL and U87-GL-EGFRvIII cell lines. i, Flow cytometry histograms showing PD-L1 expression in U87-GL and U87-GL-EGFRvIII cell lines. j, Schematic of DKO CAR-T cell library generation pipeline, including human T cell isolation and activation, CAR-T cell generation and selection, lentiviral DKO CRISPR library infection and Cas9 mRNA electroporation. Schematic in panel j created in BioRender; Chen, S. https://biorender.com/4g9xapi (2026). k, Spider plots of tumour volumes for donor 1 in vivo screen experiment shown in Fig. 1d. n = 5 biologically independent mice. l, Representative H&E-stained tumour sections from two biologically independent tumours per group from the screen shown in Fig. 1c. Scale bar, 250 μm. m, sgRNA-pair detection rates from the total library across individual samples. D, donor; T, tumour. n, Heat map of Spearman correlation coefficients between the log2-normalized counts-per-million (log-norm.) sgRNA counts for each sample. Data were arranged by hierarchical clustering using the ward.D2 method. o, Multidimensional scaling analysis of log2-normalized screen data using the top 10,000 most variable sgRNA pairs across samples. Data points were clustered by k-means. p, Box-dot plot of library representation across individual samples, showing the distribution of all sgRNA-pair constructs counts. Boxes indicate the 25th–75th percentiles, center lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Individual points represent sgRNA-pair counts. q, Empirical cumulative distribution function of DKO library representation among detected sgRNA pairs in plasmid, pre-injection cell and tumour samples. Sample labels in m-p indicate sample type, plasmid, pre-injection cell or tumour, and donor ID.

a, Distribution of the top four performing sgRNA-pair constructs for top DKO hits across samples, ranked by SAMBA sgRNA z-score. b, Heat map of DKO screen scores for all pairwise gene combinations assessed in the CRISPR screen. Values were scaled and visualized within a range of −1 to 1. Hierarchical clustering was performed using the Ward.D2 method based on Euclidean distances. c, Scatter plot showing the relationship between screen enrichment and synergistic effect. SAMBA z-scores were plotted against synergy scores for each gene pair. Dashed lines indicate FDR-adjusted P value, q < 0.05, for epistasis and SAMBA results. d, Scatter plot of observed DKO SAMBA scores versus expected SAMBA scores based on the additive effects of the corresponding SKOs for each gene pair (SKO1 + SKO2). Points are colored by synergy score. Linear regression yielded R2 = 0.0152 (n = 2,485 gene pairs; 71 SKO genes), indicating minimal predictability of DKO outcomes from SKO additivity. e, Quantification of indel frequencies in DKO-edited CAR-T cells 5 days after electroporation across three independent batches. P values were calculated using unpaired two-sided t-tests. Data are mean ± s.e.m.; n = 3 human donors. Each dot represents one human donor. f, Quantification of indel frequencies in CAR-T cells from three donors generated across three independent batches 90 days after gene editing. P values were calculated using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s multiple-comparisons test versus GTC. Data are mean + s.e.m.; n = 3 independent donor-derived CAR-T cell preparations, generated from three donors in independent batches. NS, not significant, *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001.

a, Quantification of live cells 5 days after editing in different DKO CAR-T cells compared with controls, n = 3 infection replicates per group. b, Schematic of generation of DKO CAR-T or CAR-Jurkat cell generation and downstream assays. Schematic in panel b created in BioRender; Chen, S. https://biorender.com/7vyyd1r (2026). c, Quantification of Ca2+ flux AUC and peak signal change in different DKO CAR-Jurkat samples. The resting region was defined as 1 min before antigen crosslinking, and the peak region was defined as 500 s after cross-linking. AUC is calculated as (mean peak signal – mean resting signal) × 500. E:T = 1:2. n = 3 per group per time point. f, Schematic of the NFAT/AP-1 GFP reporter structure and quantification of GFP+ cells. g, Schematic of the NF-κB CFP reporter structure and the quantification of CFP+ cells. h, Quantifications of tonic signaling in CAR-Jurkat cells after 1 month cell culture without stimulation, n = 3. P value was determined by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s correction for multiple comparisons test versus GTC. i, Left, representative flow cytometry histograms showing CD107a expression in CD8+ DKO and GTC CAR-T cells after 2-h coculture with U87-GL-EGFRvIII cells. Right, quantification of absolute CAR-T cell numbers; n = 3 on day 0, n = 6 on day 2, 5, and 7 per group. l, Quantification of CellTrace Violetlow CAR-T cells in low IL-2 medium, measured on day 7; n = 3 per group. m, Quantification of live cells percentage in culture or after repeated challenge. n, Left, quantification of CD45RO+ CD62L+ DKO CAR-T cells after two rounds of tumour stimulation on day 5. Right, quantification of CD27+ DKO CAR-T cells after two rounds of tumour stimulation on day 5; n = 6 per group. For each round of coculture, E:T = 1:4. o, Quantifications of LAG-3, PD-1, and TIM-3 expression in CAR-T cells after repeated tumour challenge on day 5, n = 4 per group. For each round of coculture, E:T = 1:4. p, Quantification of LAG-3+, PD-1+, TIM-3+ CAR-T cells after two rounds of tumour stimulation on day 5; n = 4 per group. For each round of coculture, E:T = 1:4. q, SPICE analysis of LAG-3, PD-1, and TIM-3 expression in CAR-T cells on day 5. Data in d-g,k right,m,r are mean ± s.e.m.; data in a,h-j,k left,l,n-p are mean + s.e.m. Dashed lines in c, i, j, n-p indicate mean values of the GTC group. n indicates biologically independent samples unless otherwise stated. a, Schematic of the time-series RNA-seq experiment in DKO, NR4A1 SKO, SOCS3 SKO, and GTC CAR-T cells undergoing repeated tumour challenges. b, Principal components analysis (PCA) of all RNA-seq samples across all stimulation time-points (left) or separated by timepoint (right). The first two principal components are shown. Genotypes are indicated by dot color, and samples are grouped by time point (left) or genotype (right) using convex hulls. c, Volcano plots of differential expression (DE) analysis for epistasis at each time-point. Significant epistatic transcripts were defined by an FDR-adjusted P value (q value) <0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change (LFC) > 0.5 for the DKO interaction term in the statistical model (Methods). Top DE transcripts are labeled based on significance and LFC, with selected transcripts shown in bold. d, Heatmaps and pathway analysis of DE transcripts from pairwise comparisons between genotypes across stimulation times. For each time point, DE transcripts were hierarchically clustered and shown as heatmaps (left). Pathway analyses were performed independently for each transcript cluster using over-representation analysis (ORA) tests with MSIGDB v7.4 Hallmark gene-sets. Significant pathways (q < 0.05; up to four pathways per cluster shown) are shown on the right, color-coded by the transcript clusters. #1289. Bournemouth thrash Milan to seal greatest win in club’s history

Eighteen years ago, Bournemouth were minutes away from being liquidated and playing in the fourth tier. On Thursday night, Bournemouth not only welcomed AC Milan in Europe; they did so as favourites, and then pummelled them.

When Amine Adli curled in an 84-minute free-kick with his left foot at the Vitality Stadium, it put the seal on the most extraordinary evening in Bournemouth’s history. On a brutally windy and wet night, Bournemouth trounced AC Milan 3-0.

Amine Adli with a SUPERB free-kick to give Bournemouth a 3-0 lead vs AC Milan 🚀 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/KX5i5oM3TG

Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the new European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

“It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, said. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”

Evanilson, perhaps, was Bournemouth’s standout player against AC Milan, combining intricate linkup play with a constant threat in front of goal. Centre-back Antonio Silva, controlling play from deep while marauding forward, also possessed a calmness that any of Milan’s beleaguered team lacked.

His side’s fate swiftly sealed, Amorim did not bother to summon Luka Modric or Christian Pulisic. Bournemouth’s own bench showed the depth that the club now possesses. Rayan showed off his trickery and directness; Adli – a substitute for substitute Alex Toth, who suffered a hamstring injury – then ensured that Bournemouth secured the margin of victory that their dominance deserved.

Thirty-one years ago, Patrick Kluivert scored against AC Milan in Europe. If his son Justin’s eighth-minute penalty will not receive the acclaim of Patrick’s winner for Ajax in the 1995 Champions League final, the goal will be etched in Bournemouth’s hearts.

After Evanilson’s header from a corner struck Koni De Winter’s hand, a VAR review led to Bournemouth being awarded a penalty. Kluivert eyed up Mike Maignan, and waited for the goalkeeper to dive before nonchalantly stroking the ball into the unguarded left corner.

And so Bournemouth were beating AC Milan, a scenario that would have seemed unfathomable for vast swathes of these two clubs’ existence. Even more extraordinary was how deserved the goal was: both Kluivert and Evanilson had already spurned opportunities, with Milan seeming overwhelmed by Bournemouth’s intensity.

Watching his side lack any coherence in their passing, Ruben Amorim rapidly came to look as ghoulish as in his last days at Old Trafford. Or, indeed, Michael Carrick in Como 24 hours earlier.

Amorim swiftly had cause to become more irate. Just as Milan had threatened to regain a semblance of control, Maignan inexplicably pushed Tyler Adams in the face when Bournemouth had a corner. VAR had no reason to give Maignan a reprieve from his red card, and Bournemouth’s ensuing penalty.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.
